tasks.brief:
We are adding a 16-bit sampling channel next to a 1 MHz switching digital block on an existing board. The converter digitizes a 10.000 kHz, 1.000 V peak tone for a coherent-phase measurement, and downstream averaging assumes no slow drift or offset creep in the codes. Digital return current couples into the analog ground and reference through the shared return segment. I need you to design the passive ground-bridging, decoupling and reference-filter network around the fixed lumped board model in /app/input_assets/input.json (nodes, fixed parts, source waveforms, converter law, corner list, element limits and the design file schema are all there).

Fixed: the 12 mohm + 8 nH shared segment cannot be removed; the digital block, converter and reference source cannot change; no active parts. Budget: at most 14 discrete passive parts (R, L, C; a ferrite is an R plus an L), at most 3 ground bridges, at most 4 extra internal nodes.

Definition of the quality metric: take the raw converter code series (100 kS/s, 2.0 s capture) and fit it by least squares with exactly these five terms: sine and cosine at 10.000 kHz, one constant, sine and cosine at 1.000 kHz. The residual RMS is the RMS of what remains, in LSB at the 16-bit scale. No other term is permitted in the fit.

Requirements (all over the 2 s duty ramp described in the input file, at every corner of the supply 3.15/3.30/3.45 V, trace and bridge resistance -20/+20 percent, capacitor tolerance -20/+20 percent, and at intermediate points inside those ranges):
- R1: full-capture residual RMS <= 0.30 LSB.
- R2: the same metric, fitted separately on the window 0 to 0.2 s and on the window 1.8 to 2.0 s, <= 0.30 LSB in each.
- R3: element count <= 14, bridges <= 3, every node and value within the legal sets and ranges in the input file.
- R4: mean voltage between the converter reference pin and analog ground over 0 to 0.2 s between 2.450 V and 2.500 V.

Deliver /app/output/design.json in the schema given in the input file: a list of elements, each with type, value (or r_mohm and l_nH for a bridge), node_a and node_b, using only the named nodes plus up to four internal nodes.
tasks.handbook:
Background data (ranges, practice).

LSB: the converter full scale is +/-2.5 V over 16 bits, so 1 LSB is about 76 uV at the nominal 2.5 V reference. A 1 mV reference shift changes the peak code of a 1 V tone by roughly 5 LSB. Ground shift at the converter input adds directly to the code at about 13.1 LSB per mV.

Shared-impedance coupling: a return current I through R + jwL produces I*R at low frequency and I*wL at the burst harmonics. At 1 MHz, 8 nH is about 50 mohm, four times the 12 mohm resistance. Mean digital current is duty x peak, so a duty ramp becomes a slow ramp in ground voltage across the shared resistance. A parallel path lowers the DC and low-frequency impedance. It also forms loops with the 8 nH inductance that can ring at several MHz when the damping is poor.

Aliasing: the 1 MHz burst content lies exactly at 10 x the sample rate, so every harmonic lands at DC in the sampled data. What the converter sees is the instantaneous ground and reference value at a fixed phase of the burst period, which changes as the pulse width changes.

Reference path: the reference pin is divided against the converter's 20 kohm load, so each ohm in series with the reference costs 125 uV of reference level at 2.5 V. A capacitor from the reference pin to analog ground lets the reference follow analog-ground bounce above the corner 1/(2 pi R C), which cancels the ratio error. A large RC corner also makes the reference lag slow ground movement.

Capacitors: surface-mount ceramics from 100 pF to 22 uF; electrolytics and tantalums to 470 uF. A real capacitor includes equivalent series resistance (a few mohm to tens of mohm) and inductance (about 0.5 to 1.5 nH for small packages). The checker uses the ESR and ESL stated in the input file. Ferrite beads behave as an R plus an L at these frequencies; typical values are 0.1 to 1 ohm and 50 to 500 nH, with the resistance rising with frequency.

Layout bridges: a short copper bridge of a few millimetres has about 6 to 30 mohm and 3 to 10 nH. Its resistance scales with the trace tolerance corner.

Fit conventions: the fit is ordinary linear least squares on the raw code series sampled at t_n = n x 10 us + 0.9 us, with t = 0 at the start of the capture. The residual RMS is the square root of the mean squared residual over the stated window. Codes are the unrounded real-valued converter output expressed in LSB; quantization is not included.
tasks.review:
### 19 · Mixed-signal ground/reference network for a 16-bit channel — advance, rank 8

Design decision as written: yes — "design the passive ground-bridging, decoupling and reference-filter network around the fixed lumped board model" (deliverable is a list of elements with type, value and node pair, i.e. a topology-and-values decision).

Forge task: Design a passive network (R/L/C plus up to 3 ground bridges, up to 14 discrete parts, up to 4 internal nodes) between AGND, DGND, PSU_RTN, REF_IN and REF_ADC on the fixed lumped board model, such that the exactly-five-term-fit residual RMS of the 16-bit code series is <= 0.30 LSB over the full 2 s capture and in each of the 0–0.2 s and 1.8–2.0 s windows, at every declared corner and held-out interior point, while the mean REF_ADC-to-AGND voltage stays in 2.450–2.500 V.

Why it fits:
- It is a design decision as written: the agent chooses which parts exist, their values and how they are wired; the checker evaluates the delivered file alone.
- The physical mechanism is coupled and real: lowering shared-return DC resistance (bridges) fights the duty-driven ground offset ramp, while the same bridges create L-C loops that ring at MHz and contaminate the burst-phase sampled value; the reference filter must follow ground bounce fast enough to cancel ratio error yet not lag the slow duty ramp; R4 caps how much series resistance the reference path can take. That is a genuine multi-objective trade-off, not hidden rules.
- The metric is deliberately resistant to the standard cheat: a solver that adds a linear-in-time term to its own fit absorbs the ramp and never sees the failure. The exact five-term basis is specified in the brief and in the handbook.
- Budget (14 parts, 3 bridges, 4 internal nodes) makes it a small combinatorial design, plausible for one agent run.

What stops it:
- Structural: none. The deliverable, node set, part limits and metric are specified.
- Unresolved feasibility risks: (a) the 0.30 LSB limit is explicitly provisional in the reference outline and no passing design has been demonstrated; (b) it is an author claim, not verified evidence, that an unbridged/datasheet-style design sits at about 0.7 LSB RMS — my own rough arithmetic (mean digital current ~8–24 mA through 12 mΩ gives ~1.3–3.8 LSB of ground shift at 13.1 LSB/mV, so a ~2.5 LSB p-p ramp has RMS ~0.7 LSB after removing only a constant) is consistent with that claim but is not a simulation; (c) whether 14 parts suffice at all 20+ evaluation points is undemonstrated; (d) the 5 % solver slack is an author choice and may be tighter than the disagreement between a harmonic-sweep envelope method and a direct transient; (e) a full 2 s transient with 1 MHz edges is not computationally feasible directly (2 s at ns steps ≈ 2e9 steps), so the slow/burst split in the grader plan is an approximation whose validity must be shown.

How to check it:
- ngspice or scipy state-space / complex nodal analysis: build the merged linear network (fixed elements from input.json plus the candidate design, including per-C ESR 5 mΩ and ESL 0.8 nH); solve slow content with a transient on the duty-ramp envelope and burst content as harmonic phasors up to ~300 MHz scaled by instantaneous duty and amplitude; sample at t_n = n*10e-6 + 0.9e-6.
- numpy: ordinary least squares with exactly [sin(2*pi*10k t), cos(2*pi*10k t), 1, sin(2*pi*1k t), cos(2*pi*1k t)] and residual RMS in LSB per window.
- A plain Python legality script: counts R/L/C and BRIDGE entries, checks node names against {AGND, DGND, PSU_RTN, REF_IN, REF_ADC, N1..N4}, checks value ranges and bridge minima, counts a ferrite as two parts.
- Cross-check the two solution routes (ngspice transient vs scipy state-space vs harmonic superposition) on one test network to establish that the 5 % slack is adequate.

Simulation gaps:
- The model is lumped: no plane geometry, no distributed return paths, no via/package inductance, no coupling beyond the two named trace segments, no discrete-L self-resonance or DCR (discrete R and L are declared ideal, which is optimistic at 300 MHz), no capacitor dielectric/temperature/voltage derating and no ESR/ESL cornering.
- Sources are ideal; the converter law is memoryless with no quantization, jitter, INL/DNL or aperture effects; "initial state = steady state at duty 0.2" is a modelling convenience.
- Harmonic superposition plus an instantaneous-duty envelope assumes the network is linear and that the duty ramp is slow relative to burst settling; this needs validating against a shorter direct transient on a reduced time base.
- Manufacturability/assembly is not simulated at all: legality of values and bridge ranges stands in for it.

Why frontier models fail: plausible but a hypothesis until trials exist. The traps are engineering-real: the exact five-term basis forbids absorbing the ramp, so a self-consistent but weakened metric cannot be used as the solver's own fitness; the aliasing (1 MHz burst harmonics land at DC at 100 kS/s, sampled at a fixed burst phase) means only the instantaneous burst-phase ground and reference values matter, which is easy to get subtly wrong; and the reference-filter corner trades ramp-following against ripple rejection under a hard R4 DC window, so a design that looks good on one metric usually breaks another. Subject to: an actual trial run showing a frontier model's proxy metric passing while the exact basis fails.

Real-world risks:
- A design passing the lumped model would likely behave qualitatively as intended on a real board, but the gap is large: real shared-return geometry, plane resonances, package parasitics and converter PSRR/INR can dominate at the 76 uV/LSB level.
- The bridge model (6–30 mohm, 3–10 nH per handbook) is a range, not a measured geometry; the delivered network names no copper widths or lengths.
- Ceramic C of tens of uF loses capacitance with DC bias; the 20 % capacitor corner may not cover that.

Milestones (if too big): none required; the task plausibly fits one run. If runtime proves prohibitive, split as: 1. surrogate builder + baseline reproduction: implement the code-series/fit metric, reproduce the ~0.7 LSB unbridged baseline — grader checks the reproduced RMS matches the stated figure within tolerance. 2. network search over the 14-part budget — grader checks the four requirements at all corners.

What to change (reshape): nothing structural. Pin down the open items below instead.

Numbers to supply next:
- Requirement: residual-RMS limit — confirm 0.30 LSB after calibration; first reproduce the author's ~0.7 LSB unbridged baseline and demonstrate at least one design passing all four requirements (verification still needed, not just a specification). Example value: 0.30 LSB RMS with 5 % numerical slack.
- Requirement: bridge element bounds — bridge_r_mohm_max and bridge_l_nH_max (handbook implies 6–30 mohm and 3–10 nH; state the maxima the checker accepts, e.g. 30 and 10).
- Requirement: parasitic policy for discrete R and L — confirm ideal up to 300 MHz or supply a self-resonant-frequency/DCR model; confirm ESR/ESL of capacitors are cornered or fixed at 5 mohm / 0.8 nH.
- Interface: input at /app/input_assets/input.json, output at /app/output/design.json; example entry e.g. {"type":"C","value":2.2e-05,"node_a":"AGND","node_b":"PSU_RTN"} and {"type":"BRIDGE","r_mohm":8,"l_nH":5,"node_a":"AGND","node_b":"PSU_RTN"}; state that C values are in farads as decimals and whether negative values / zero are rejected.
- Handbook data: already largely supplied (1 LSB ≈ 76 uV; 13.1 LSB/mV ground sensitivity; 125 uV per ohm in the reference path; ferrite 0.1–1 ohm and 50–500 nH). Add the accepted capacitor ESR/ESL corner and any derating factors.
- Verification still needed: solver cross-validation (ngspice vs scipy vs harmonic superposition) on a test network; measured runtime for one full 20-point evaluation; validation of the slow/burst envelope split against a direct transient; check that the steady-state initial condition at duty 0.2 is reproducible; confirm the 8 held-out interior points are seed-reproducible.

Evidence status: draft-only input. All figures (the 0.7 LSB baseline, the ~2x shortfall, public-design failures, budget fit, the 5 % slack and the mechanism narrative) are author claims; the embedded input.json text establishes supplied text, not that the asset exists or that any simulation has been run. The reference outline is a proposed solution, not a passing design. No artifact or measurement has been inspected; nothing here is verified.

Checks before full-task readiness: 1) confirm /app/input_assets/input.json exists and matches the embedded text byte-for-byte in the fields the grader reads; 2) reproduce the unbridged baseline residual (~0.7 LSB claimed) with the exact five-term basis; 3) demonstrate one passing design at all 12 corners plus the 8 held-out points; 4) cross-validate two independent solvers and confirm the 5 % slack bounds their disagreement; 5) measure the runtime of one full evaluation; 6) supply bridge maxima and the discrete-parasitic policy.

tasks.brief:
I need a transconductance cell for a sensor front end, delivered as a SPICE subcircuit. A slow offset-trim loop removes the input-pair mismatch offset. It has to settle fast, stay well behaved and stay quiet while the cell amplifies a 50 kHz to 200 kHz signal.

Interface: `.subckt gm_cell inp inn outp outn vdd` (ground is node 0). Supply is 1.8 V +/-5 %. The PMOS input pair is named M1 (inp side) and M2 (inn side), with W and L on their instance lines. Use the models pch and nch from the supplied models file and do not redefine them. Each input is driven through 250 kOhm at 0.8 V common mode. Each output is held at 1.0 V with 2 pF to ground. Iout is the current into outp minus the current into outn. The input-referred pair offset is zero-mean with sigma = 5.66 mV*um / sqrt(W*L) of M1/M2, and I will use draws out to +/-3 sigma. Trim correction must enter as a series voltage in the input path. It must come through the supplied trimact block, instantiated exactly once; that block drives only controlled-source control inputs. Other allowed elements are MOSFETs, resistors, capacitors, ideal controlled sources and ideal DC current sources. Every resistor and capacitor, including those in trimact, can vary +/-10 % from nominal.

Requirements, with a 20 mV peak differential sine input unless stated:
- R1: fundamental of Iout divided by input amplitude, at any frequency 50 kHz to 200 kHz, must be 0.97 to 1.03 mS.
- R2: steady-state residual input-referred offset (mean Iout / gm) must be <= 150 uV.
- R3: after power-up (supply ramping from 0, integrator uncharged), the cycle-averaged input-referred offset must enter 150 uV and stay there within <= 200 us of the supply reaching 90 %.
- R4: after a +/-5 mV input offset step, the cycle-averaged offset must settle to within 1 % of the step of its final value in <= 200 us.
- R5: overshoot after that step must be <= 20 % of the step.
- R6: HD3 must be <= -60 dBc at any frequency 50 kHz to 200 kHz.
- R7: with a 10 uV peak sinusoidal offset wander at any frequency 2 kHz to 5 kHz in series with the input, the Iout spectral line at the wander frequency must be <= -72 dBc relative to the fundamental of a 100 kHz signal.
- R8: that wander line must agree to within 1 dB between consecutive windows of at least 10 wander periods.
- R9: the R4 settling time must change by <= 10 us between two otherwise identical evaluations of the same record at different numerical resolution.
- R10: the peak trim voltage at the trimact output must stay within +/-9 mV through R3 to R5, including mismatch plus step.
- R11: mean supply current from vdd must be <= 180 uA (20 uA is reserved for trim circuitry outside the netlist).

All limits must hold over supply corners, the stated component tolerance and any mismatch draw within +/-3 sigma.

Deliver /app/output/gm_cell.cir: a SPICE netlist containing the gm_cell subcircuit and nothing that needs other files except the supplied models and trimact definitions. The supplied files are in /app/input_assets/. Measurement conventions are in the handbook.
tasks.handbook:
# Handbook

## Fixed data
Models (models.lib, level-1 square-law): NMOS vto 0.45 V, kp 220 uA/V^2, lambda 0.08/V. PMOS vto -0.45 V, kp 80 uA/V^2, lambda 0.10/V. tox 4 nm (Cox about 8.6 fF/um^2), overlap caps 0.3 fF/um. Minimum L is 0.18 um. Gate area and device sizes are free. Temperature is 27 C; ignore temperature effects.

trimact (trim_actuator.cir): ports `cin vtrim`. It is a unity-gain buffer followed by two cascaded RC low-passes with time constants 8 us and 16 us, and models the trim DAC and reconstruction filter. The output must not be loaded other than by a controlled-source control input. Series insertion into the input path is commonly done with a voltage-controlled voltage source whose controlling voltage is v(vtrim).

## Offset mismatch
Pelgrom: sigma(deltaVT) = sqrt(2) * A_VT / sqrt(W*L) for a matched pair, with A_VT = 4 mV*um and W, L in um. Offset is injected as a DC source in series with inp, outside the cell, after the 250 kOhm. Draws are uniform to +/-3 sigma, which means larger gate area lowers the offset the trim must remove. Gate capacitance forms a pole with the 250 kOhm input resistance, so large area costs gm flatness at 200 kHz.

## Practice and ranges
A square-law differential pair has gm = Itail/Vov with Vov per device. Its third-order distortion for a sine of amplitude A scales as HD3 ~ (A*gm/Itail)^2/16 and improves with degeneration only if the gm target is held. Source degeneration trades gm and linearity against headroom. Typical trim loops use an integrator, optionally with a proportional path, and a series sense filter, giving crossover in the 2 to 20 kHz range with phase margin 30 to 75 degrees. The sensitivity peaking of a loop with phase margin PM is roughly 1/(2*sin(PM/2)). Current can be sensed with a 0 V source in series with a drain. Behavioural integrators can be built from a VCCS or CCCS into a capacitor.

## Measurement definitions
- Iout = I(into outp) - I(into outn), measured on the source holding each output at 1.0 V.
- Cycle-averaged input-referred offset e(t): the mean of Iout over the trailing one input period, divided by the measured fundamental gm at that frequency.
- gm: fundamental Fourier amplitude of Iout in a coherent, integer-cycle window starting at least 1.5 ms after power-up, divided by the input amplitude.
- Residual offset: mean of Iout in the same window divided by gm.
- Power-up settling: time after the supply reaches 90 % of its final value until |e| stays <= 150 uV for the rest of a 1.5 ms record. Supply ramp times of 2 to 20 us are used.
- Step settling: step applied at 1 ms; final value is the mean of e over 1.8 to 2.0 ms; settling time is the last instant |e - final| exceeds 1 % of |step|. Overshoot is the peak excess of e beyond the final value in the direction of travel, divided by |step|.
- HD3: amplitude of the third harmonic over the fundamental, in dBc, in a coherent window.
- Wander line: Fourier amplitude of Iout at the wander frequency divided by the fundamental amplitude, in dBc. Windows are integer-cycle in both frequencies; the wander is added in series with the signal and the DC offset.
- Numerical resolution comparison: the whole record is evaluated twice, the second time with the maximum time step halved relative to the first.
- Corner set: supply 1.71, 1.8, 1.89 V; R and C values scaled by 0.9 or 1.1 independently (four combinations); mismatch draws in +/-3 sigma including the extremes; two different supply ramp rates.

## Fixed testbench loads
The 1.0 V output sources and the 2 pF capacitors per output are outside the cell. The cell input pins see the source resistance and the offset sources.
tasks.review:
### 25 · Offset-trimmed gm cell with datasheet-style limits — advance, rank 8

Design decision as written: yes — "I need a transconductance cell for a sensor front end, delivered as a SPICE subcircuit" with free topology and sizing inside an allowed element set and fixed interface (`.subckt gm_cell inp inn outp outn vdd`).

Forge task: Design a PMOS-input differential transconductance cell plus a slow series-injected offset-trim loop (fixed `trimact` actuator instantiated once) as a ngspice subcircuit meeting R1-R11: gm 0.97-1.03 mS across 50-200 kHz, residual offset <= 150 uV, power-up and +/-5 mV step settling <= 200 us with <= 20 % overshoot, HD3 <= -60 dBc, a 2-5 kHz offset-wander line <= -72 dBc stable to 1 dB between windows, settling-time shift <= 10 us when the max time step is halved, trim voltage within +/-9 mV, and mean supply current <= 180 uA, all over supply 1.71/1.8/1.89 V, R/C scaled 0.9/1.1 independently, mismatch draws to +/-3 sigma, and two supply ramp rates.

Why it fits:
• Circuit synthesis with parameter freedom is exactly the forge category: the deliverable is geometry/topology in a netlist, and every limit is a number a script can extract.
• ngspice is a listed tool and covers all of it: transient for settling/overshoot/trim peak/supply current, FFT over coherent integer-cycle windows for gm, HD3 and the wander line, rerun with halved max step for R9.
• The hard part is genuinely engineering-coupled: gate area trades mismatch (Pelgrom sigma) against the 250 kOhm input pole and gm flatness; loop crossover trades wander rejection (R7 pushes it to roughly the 9-12 kHz region, per the author's inference) against phase margin through the fixed 8/16 us trimact poles and thus overshoot (R5), settling (R3/R4) and window-to-window wander agreement (R8); source degeneration trades HD3 against the 180 uA budget and headroom at 1.8 V with outputs at 1.0 V.
• The interface, allowed element set, mismatch injection point and measurement conventions are specified tightly enough that a grader can accept any obeying topology.

What stops it:
• Structural: nothing. It is a design task, simulatable end to end with open tools.

tasks.brief:
We are adding a ruggedised ultrasonic proximity transducer to an existing control board and need the passive interface between the excitation driver and the transducer port. The driver is a 5 V peak sine source with 50 ohm output impedance. Its frequency drifts with temperature anywhere in 194 kHz to 206 kHz. The transducer is lightly damped, and a surge clamp sits permanently across its port. The transducer and clamp models are in /app/input_assets/fixed_parts.cir. Do not modify them. Amplitude at the transducer must stay steady and clean at every frequency in the band, because a ring-up that drifts or never settles corrupts the sensor reading.

Fixed interface: your network is a subcircuit named IFACE with ports IN, OUT, GND. The source drives IN through its 50 ohm. OUT connects to the transducer port, where the clamp also connects. GND is the common return. The network is passive, R, L and C elements only, ideal, at most 10 elements. Values must sit on standard grids: E24 for resistors (1% tolerance), E12 for capacitors (2%) and E12 for inductors (2%). Series or parallel combinations are allowed.

Scope: unless a requirement says otherwise, every requirement holds at every frequency in 194 kHz to 206 kHz, both with nominal parts and with every element at any value inside its stated tolerance. Voltages are at OUT relative to GND.
1. Fundamental amplitude between 3.6 V and 4.7 V peak, measured in steady state.
2. Total harmonic distortion (harmonics 2 to 10 relative to the fundamental) of at most 1.0 percent.
3. Burst start: the envelope is within 2 percent of its final value within 20 source cycles, from a zero initial state and from a transducer starting with 20 mA motional current and 10 V on its motional capacitor.
4. Periodicity: after 60 cycles, the waveform differs from itself shifted by 10 cycles by at most 0.5 percent RMS, relative to the RMS of the waveform.
5. Burst end: when the source drops to zero after an 80-cycle burst, the peak of OUT in the 15th source cycle after the drop (cycle 15 counting the first cycle after the drop as cycle 1) is below 5 percent of the steady amplitude.
6. Resistor power: with the source running at any band frequency, each resistor dissipates at most 0.25 W average in steady state, nominal parts and tolerance extremes.
7. Build limits: only R, L and C, at most 10 elements, values on the stated grids.

Deliverables under /app/output/:
- interface.cir: a SPICE netlist containing the .subckt IFACE IN OUT GND definition and whatever is needed to run it.
- design.json: fields topology_tag (short string) and components (list of objects with ref, type R, L or C, and value in SI units), matching the netlist.
tasks.handbook:
## Fixed parts (as in fixed_parts.cir)
Transducer: series Rm 300 ohm, Lm 9.55 mH, Cm 66.3 pF (series resonance about 200 kHz, bare Q about 40) in parallel with a 470 pF port capacitance. The antiresonance is near 213 kHz. The clamp is two anti-parallel strings of five identical diodes (IS 1e-12, N 1.8, RS 1 ohm, CJO 4 pF, BV 30 V). Each string starts conducting noticeably at about 4.5 to 5 V peak, and the current rises roughly tenfold per 8 percent rise in voltage amplitude.

## Useful background
- Power available from the source into a matched load is Vpk^2/(8*50) = 62.5 mW. Voltage at a resistive port of equivalent parallel resistance Rp cannot exceed sqrt(2*P*Rp).
- The motional branch is driven from the Thevenin impedance of the source plus network. The envelope time constant is 2L/(Rm+Rth), and loaded Q = omega*L/(Rm+Rth).
- A lossless reactive network can transform the 50 ohm source to a higher effective source resistance, which sets loaded Q and amplitude together.
- Frequency drift of 3 percent either side is a large fraction of the bare transducer bandwidth (about 5 kHz).
- Ideal elements: no parasitics. Source phase starts at zero at burst start.

## Measurement definitions
- Steady state: analysed over a window of 20 whole source cycles starting after cycle 60.
- Fundamental amplitude: the peak amplitude of the Fourier component at the drive frequency over that window.
- THD: sqrt(sum of squared harmonic amplitudes, orders 2 to 10) divided by the fundamental amplitude.
- Envelope: the peak absolute value of OUT in each source cycle. The envelope settles at cycle N if it stays within 2 percent of its steady-state value from cycle N onward.
- Periodicity error: RMS of (v(t) - v(t - 10T)) over a 10-cycle window starting after cycle 60, divided by the RMS of v over the same window.
- Ring-down: the envelope after the source is set to 0 V, relative to the steady amplitude just before.
- Tolerance corners: each element independently takes any value in [nominal*(1-tol), nominal*(1+tol)], including all-low, all-high and mixed extremes.
- Held-out frequencies: points inside 194 to 206 kHz not necessarily on a regular grid, including the centre and band edges.

## Standard series
E12 (1.0 1.2 1.5 1.8 2.2 2.7 3.3 3.9 4.7 5.6 6.8 8.2) and E24 (those plus 1.1 1.3 1.6 2.0 2.4 3.0 3.6 4.3 5.1 6.2 7.5 9.1), times decades. The series come from IEC 60063.

## Practice
A design checked only at a few nominal frequencies, with thresholds placed just inside the limits, is fragile. Frequency offsets, tolerances and different numerical step sizes all move the operating point. Amplitude, clamp conduction and settling interact because the diode current depends exponentially on amplitude.
tasks.review:
### 03-03 · Passive drive interface for a clamped ultrasonic transducer across a drifting band — advance, rank 8

Design decision as written: yes — "need the passive interface between the excitation driver and the transducer port" with "Values must sit on standard grids ... at most 10 elements", delivered as ".subckt IFACE IN OUT GND" plus "design.json: fields topology_tag (short string) and components". The agent designs a network; it is not asked to analyse or measure a fixed circuit.

Forge task: Design a passive R/L/C network (max 10 elements, E24 resistors / E12 L and C, SI values) between a 5 V-peak, 50 ohm driver and a lightly damped ~200 kHz transducer with a permanent 10-diode antiparallel clamp, so that across 194–206 kHz and all element tolerance corners the OUT fundamental stays 3.6–4.7 V peak, THD(2–10) <= 1.0%, envelope settles within 2% in <= 20 source cycles from both zero and residual transducer state, 10-cycle periodicity error <= 0.5%, the 15th post-burst cycle peak < 5% of steady amplitude, and every resistor dissipates <= 0.25 W; deliver interface.cir and design.json.

Why it fits:
• Physical design decision: topology and parameter selection for a real board-level interface, with a fixed external system (source, transducer, clamp) the network must be designed against.
• Fully checkable in principle: every requirement is a waveform/power quantity obtainable from headless ngspice transients plus FFT and per-element power averaging.
• Coupled trade-offs give real difficulty: loaded Q sets band flatness, amplitude ceiling, settling and ring-down simultaneously, while the diode clamp couples amplitude exponentially to THD.
• Bounded output: <= 10 ideal elements, explicit schema (topology_tag + components list) cross-checkable against the netlist.
• Internal arithmetic in the brief is self-consistent (my check: series resonance 200.7 kHz, bare Q ~40, port Z ~290-j51 ohm at 200 kHz, P_avail = 25/(8*50) = 62.5 mW) — these are my computations from the stated model, not verified simulation.

What stops it:
• Structural, spec-vs-check gap: R1–R6 say 'every element at any value inside its stated tolerance' (an uncountable corner set). G2/G4/G6 sample 40 draws; a pass on samples does not establish the universal claim. Either narrow the requirement to the named corner/sample set or add an interval/sensitivity argument.
• Unresolved budget risk (arithmetic, not measured): a G2-equivalent sweep is roughly 375 transients x 2 timesteps (each ~80 cycles at T/1000, nonlinear diodes) — plausibly 15–125 minutes of solver time for one gate, before G4/G6 and before the agent's own design sweeps. Runtime per run must be measured before claiming a two-hour fit.
• Unverified assets and claims: /app/input_assets/fixed_parts.cir is text supplied in the draft; I have not inspected the filesystem or run it. The reference outline, the four 'public designs fail' statements, the 'tenfold current rise per 8% amplitude' figure and the provisional 4.2–4.4 V centre amplitude are author claims. (My own level-1 diode estimate for five series junctions gives a current factor of order 5–10 per 8% string-voltage rise, so the claim is order-consistent but unverified.)
• Residual-state IC specification is ambiguous: '20 mA motional current and 10 V on its motional capacitor' needs an explicit sign/direction convention and an ngspice-usable application method (.ic on named internal nodes vs. injected sources).
• Feasibility tension to demonstrate, not assume: the 3.6 V floor and 4.7 V ceiling differ by only 1.3x while the ceiling sits at clamp onset (~4.5–5 V), so tolerance-robust margin may be thin. A passing reference must be shown before this is treated as achievable.

How to check it:
• ngspice: transient of 5 V-peak sine through 50 ohm into IFACE + XDUCER + CLAMP at OUT; FFT over 20 whole cycles after cycle 60 for R1 (fundamental) and R2 (harmonics 2–10); per-cycle peak envelope for R3 (both initial states); RMS of v(t)-v(t-10T) over a 10-cycle window for R4; 80-cycle burst then source = 0 with peak in the 15th post-drop cycle for R5; resistor average power over 20 cycles for R6. Take the worse of T/400 and T/1000 steps.
• Python parser for R7 (ports, R/L/C only, <= 10 elements, E12/E24 grid with 0.5% slack, design.json consistent with netlist).
• Reproduce one baseline failure (e.g. direct drive: expected settling ~40 cycles vs 20-cycle limit) and demonstrate one passing design before freezing thresholds.

Simulation gaps:
• Ideal elements: no parasitic ESR/ESL/self-capacitance, no inductor saturation or tolerance asymmetry; real parts will shift resonance and Q.
• Level-1 diode model only (IS, N, RS, CJO, BV): junction grading, self-heating, leakage spread and clamp tolerance are absent; BV=30 V is far from the operating point so clamping onset accuracy rests on N/RS.
• Transducer model is fixed and idealised (fixed Rm/Lm/Cm/Cp, no mechanical coupling, no drift with temperature, no unit-to-unit spread) even though the brief's premise is a drifting driver — temperature drift of the transducer itself is not modelled.
• Transient numerics: timestep sensitivity, diode convergence, initial-condition loading and FFT window/whole-cycle alignment can move extracted metrics by more than the stated margins; two timesteps reduce but do not bound this error.
• Tolerance sampling is discrete; no proof over the continuous box. Held-out frequencies are random draws, not a guarantee over the band.

Why frontier models fail:
• Plausible, subject to trials: the correct operating point sits inside a narrow coupled window — flatness over a 6% band forces loaded Q <= ~8, while amplitude margin, clamp conduction (exponential in amplitude), settling from a residual state and ring-down all move together. Naive moves (raise Q for amplitude, conjugate-match to 300 ohm, resistive damping) each break a different gate, and a centre-tuned design that passes nominal grid points usually fails on held-out frequencies, tolerance draws or a different timestep. This is a hypothesis about model failure modes, not a measured result.

Real-world risks:
• Ideal-element designs may not survive real inductor tolerance, DCR, self-resonance near 200 kHz and capacitor C0G/X7R derating; E12 snapping via series/parallel pairs eats the 10-element budget.
• Clamp conduction near the amplitude ceiling risks heating and long-term diode parameter drift; no thermal/energy rating is specified.
• Driver output impedance is assumed purely 50 ohm and resistive; source phase at burst start is prescribed as zero — real driver phase/start-up jitter is unmodelled.
• A design validated only on the supplied fixed transducer may fail against transducer unit spread; a real build needs measured impedance data over temperature.

Milestones (if too big): 1. Schematic-level topology + grid-snapped values: grader checks R1/R2/R6 at 3 band + 12 held-out frequencies, nominal only. 2. Full transient/robustness pass: R3/R4/R5 plus tolerance draws and dual timestep. Only split if measured solver runtime forces it.

What to change (reshape): none required at Stage 1. Pin down the tolerance quantifier (named corner set vs. universal claim) and the residual-state sign convention in the full task text rather than reshaping the device or the core decision.

Evidence status: Draft-only input. Fixed-part netlist text, handbook values, reference outline, public-design failure claims and mechanism_survival text are author claims; my resonance/Q/impedance/power figures are my own arithmetic from the stated model and are not simulation-verified. No filesystem inspection, no ngspice execution, no runtime measurement, no passing reference design observed. tasks.brief:
We are adding a precision sensor front end behind a 12 V to 3.3 V point-of-load buck stage. Slow drift of the ripple envelope against the clock would alias into the sensor band, so we need a bound on the output residual. The power stage and loop architecture are fixed by the board; only the passive and compensator values are yours.

Fixed: synchronous buck, one inductor, one output capacitor bank, a three-pole/two-zero voltage-mode compensator, fixed-amplitude PWM ramp, fs = 500 kHz. Vin 9 to 15 V, Vout 3.3 V, load 0.2 to 2.0 A. Fixed parts (MOSFET Rds(on), dead time, ramp amplitude, divider, reference, allowed Isat list, inductor DCR) are in /app/input_assets/fixed_params.json. Inductor: L(i) = L0/(1+(i/Isat)^2), L0 0.47 to 4.7 uH, Isat from the allowed list, with Isat tolerance corners -30% and +10%. Total output capacitance at most 100 uF nominal.

Corner set, applied to every requirement below: ESR = 5 mOhm and 15 mOhm (each applied to every capacitor in the bank, replacing the ESR you chose), crossed with capacitance at 1.0x and 0.6x of the nominal value (-40% DC-bias derating), crossed with Isat at -30% and +10% of your chosen value.

Metric (residual): take the output voltage over a 200-cycle (400 us) window, least-squares fit it on exactly the basis {1, cos(2 pi fs t), sin(2 pi fs t)}, no other term, and take the RMS of what remains, in mV.

Requirements, at every corner above:
1. Steady state at Vin 9, 12, 15 V and load 0.2, 1.0, 2.0 A, window 2.0 to 2.4 ms after startup: residual RMS <= 4.0 mV.
2. Load step 0.2 A to 2.0 A at 10 A/us, Vin 12 V, from steady state: from the start of the load edge until 700 us after it, the output stays within +/-3% of 3.3 V; and residual RMS <= 4.0 mV over the 200 cycles from 300 to 700 us after the edge.
3. Light-load boundary, load 0.2 to 0.5 A at any Vin in range, whatever conduction mode results: residual RMS <= 4.0 mV (same window as 1).
4. Saturation: Isat at -30%, Vin 15 V, load 2.0 A, with ESR and capacitance corners: residual RMS <= 4.0 mV.
5. Intermediate Vin and load points inside the stated ranges must also meet requirement 1.
6. Component values must respect the bounds above, and the fixed parts and fs in the netlist must match the input file.

Netlist interface: the input source is a voltage source named Vin and the load is a current source named Iload (both to be replaced or re-valued by us), the output node is named vout, and the capacitor bank is elements named Cbank1, Cbank2, ... each with a series resistor named Rbank1, ... Inductor value and Isat are .param entries L0 and Isat.

Deliver in /app/output/: converter.cir, a SPICE netlist of the complete converter and compensator with the fixed parts as given; and design.json with fields L0_uH, Isat_A, cap_bank (list of {C_uF, ESR_mOhm}), and compensator values (resistors in ohm, capacitors in F, named as in the netlist).
tasks.handbook: Practice notes. Buck: D ~ Vout/Vin; inductor ripple dI = Vout(1-D)/(L fs). Saturation: L falls by half at i = Isat, so peak current dI/2 + Iload matters at 15 V, 2 A. Ceramic capacitors lose 40-60% capacitance at DC bias; the stated derating is a 0.6x multiplier on nominal. Output ripple ~ dI*ESR plus dI/(8 fs C). Voltage-mode type-III compensation: two zeros near the LC double-pole (about 1/(2 pi sqrt(L C))), poles at the ESR zero and about half fs; crossover typically fs/10 to fs/6 with phase margin above 45 degrees. Saturation lowers L and so shifts the LC resonance upward and reduces the damping seen by the loop; marginal loops show subharmonic or beat envelopes that move slowly relative to the clock. Light load can enter discontinuous conduction (the synchronous stage may allow reverse current; whichever the netlist implements is acceptable). Residual definition: after offset and fs terms are removed, anything else, including slow envelope or drift, remains in the residual; use uniform sampling of at least 40 points per cycle and a window of exactly 200 switching periods (400 us). Startup time zero is when Vin is applied or the soft-start begins. The inductor may be modelled with a flux-based or behavioural current-dependent inductance. Use the fixed-params values for Rds(on), dead time, ramp and divider; sense_divider_ratio = vref/vout. Typical vendor datasheet buck designs use L0 1-2.2 uH, 47-100 uF output and crossover about 50 kHz. Units in fixed_params.json: Hz, V, A, mOhm, ns, uH, uF.

### 21-buck-pol-ripple-residual-saturating-inductor · POL buck with bounded residual under saturation corners — advance, rank 8

Design decision as written: yes — "The power stage and loop architecture are fixed by the board; only the passive and compensator values are yours."

Forge task: Select L0 (0.47-4.7 uH), an allowed Isat, a capacitor bank (<= 100 uF nominal) and type-III compensator values for a 12 V->3.3 V, 500 kHz synchronous buck, delivering converter.cir and design.json, such that the residual RMS of vout (offset plus one fs sinusoid removed) stays <= 4.0 mV and the load-step excursion stays within +/-3% at every ESR(5/15 mOhm) x C(1.0x/0.6x) x Isat(-30%/+10%) corner.

Why it fits:
• The deliverable is a set of physical component values plus a working netlist, not an analysis or a report; the agent must make a trade-off (inductance vs saturation vs capacitance vs loop shape) and stand behind it.
• The metric is exactly specified: uniform sampling, 200-cycle windows, fixed basis {1, cos, sin} at fs, RMS of the remainder — fully scriptable in Python after an ngspice run.
• Corner set, netlist interface (Vin, Iload, vout, Cbank*/Rbank*, .param L0/Isat) and output schema (design.json fields) are given, so the grader can override corners deterministically.
• Real engineering coupling: at Vin 15 V, 2 A the ripple current is large relative to the -30% Isat corner, so L falls, the LC resonance moves, and the loop margin and residual move with it — this is the kind of coupled trade frontier models get wrong without iteration.

What stops it:
• Structural objection: none. Fixing the power stage and compensator architecture is a stated constraint, not an uncheckable step.
• Unresolved feasibility risk (not a missing number): the 4.0 mV residual threshold is described by the author as provisional until a reference design is simulated; with ~3-3.5 A ripple at 15 V and 15 mOhm ESR the non-fundamental ripple content is on the order of a few mV, so the margin may be thin or absent. Author's reference_outline is a proposed solution, not a passing design.
• Unresolved feasibility risk: a behavioural current-dependent inductor L(i)=L0/(1+(i/Isat)^2) plus ideal-ish synchronous switches and dead time can be slow or non-convergent in ngspice at 500 kHz over 2.4 ms windows; no measured runtime is supplied.
• Unresolved feasibility risk: the author's claim that a solver's own residual proxy can mask subharmonic envelopes is unverified; the fixed-basis grader metric itself is well defined, but the marginal-design failure modes it is meant to catch have not been demonstrated in simulation.

How to check it:
• ngspice (.tran, timestep small enough for 40+ points per 2 us cycle): produce vout at each Vin x load x corner; verify switching frequency, output level and the step response shape.
• Python/numpy: uniform resampling, least-squares fit on exactly {1, cos(2 pi fs t), sin(2 pi fs t)}, RMS of residual in the stated windows (2.0-2.4 ms; 300-700 us post-step).
• Static parse (Python) of converter.cir and design.json: L0 range, Isat list membership, total nominal C <= 100 uF, fs = 500 kHz, fixed Rds(on)/dead time/ramp/divider values, presence of Vin/Iload/vout/Cbank*/Rbank*/.param L0/Isat, and consistency between design.json and the netlist.
• Checkable in principle; not implemented or validated here. Unverified: solver convergence rate, behavioural-inductor accuracy vs a flux-based model, timestep sensitivity of the residual RMS at the 2% tolerance level, and runtime of the full corner sweep.

Simulation gaps:
• No thermal, core loss, capacitor aging/leakage, MOSFET switching loss or board-layout parasitics; ESR is a fixed resistor per capacitor and the ESR zero's interaction with ESL/decoupling is not modelled.
• DCM/reverse-current behaviour of the synchronous stage depends on how the agent implements the switches; a simplified model may under- or over-state light-load residual (R3).
• Startup and soft-start detail is only loosely defined ("time zero is when Vin is applied or the soft-start begins"); window 2.0-2.4 ms must have reached steady state in every corner, which is not demonstrated.

Why frontier models fail:
• The residual metric punishes exactly the behaviour models tend to wave away: slow beat/subharmonic envelopes near saturation and light load that a hand calculation or a single nominal simulation misses.
• Eight corners must hold simultaneously while the step requirement penalises over-damping and R4 penalises under-sized inductors — a genuine multi-constraint trade that only a real simulation loop resolves. (Predicted failure is a hypothesis; supporting trials are not supplied.)

Real-world risks:
• Inductor peak current at 15 V/2 A with -30% Isat sits close to the allowed list's lower options; saturation and DCR heating in the built unit may exceed the behavioural model.
• The chosen capacitance assumes a -40% DC-bias derating multiplier; real MLCC derating depends on part number, voltage rating and aging.
• Residual measured on an ideal netlist can be smaller than on hardware with switching-node coupling and ESL.

Milestones (if too big): not required; the task plausibly fits one run once runtime is measured. If it does not, split: 1. power-stage netlist + L(i) law: grader checks topology, fixed parts, fs and converter open-loop operation. 2. Compensator + corners: grader checks R1/R3/R4/R5 residuals. 3. Load-step: grader checks R2 excursion and residual.

What to change (reshape): nothing structural. Pin down, in the numbers below: threshold calibration against a reference simulation, the exact ESR-override rule, inductor-current definition in the L(i) law, and transient settings that make the residual reproducible within the stated 2% tolerance.

Numbers to supply next:
• Requirement: residual RMS threshold at each corner class — e.g. 4.0 mV, to be confirmed by simulating at least one reference design (e.g. L0 1.5 uH, 6 A Isat, 70 uF) and reporting its worst-corner residual; if the reference fails, recalibrate before release rather than widening the limit silently.
• Requirement: load-step edge definition and step source — e.g. current ramp 0.2 -> 2.0 A at 10 A/us with edge time t_edge specified as an absolute time in the netlist (e.g. 2.0 ms).
• Requirement: steady-state convergence criterion before the 2.0-2.4 ms window — e.g. |dvout/dt| < 1 mV over 100 us prior.
• Interface: /app/input_assets/fixed_params.json as supplied (values confirmed, units Hz/V/A/mOhm/ns/uH/uF); /app/output/converter.cir (ASCII SPICE, ngspice-compatible, .tran directive supplied by grader) and /app/output/design.json with keys L0_uH (float), Isat_A (float from [2.5,3.5,4.5,6.0]), cap_bank (list of {C_uF, ESR_mOhm}), compensator (map of element name -> value).
• Interface: grader override convention — e.g. RbankN .param values replaced by 5 or 15 mOhm, CbankN scaled by 1.0 or 0.6, .param Isat scaled by 0.7 or 1.1; state that design.json must agree with converter.cir element values exactly.
• Handbook data: inductor law convention — e.g. L(i) = L0/(1+(i/Isat)^2) evaluated on instantaneous inductor current, implemented flux-based or behaviourally as the agent chooses, with a required self-test (measured effective L within 5% of the law at 0.5x, 1x, 2x Isat); plus inductor DCR 8 mOhm, capacitor DC-bias multiplier 0.6, dead time 10 ns, ramp 1.2 V, vref 0.8 V as in fixed_params.json.
• Verification still needed (not specifications): measure full-sweep runtime and residual RMS noise vs timestep; reproduce at least one of the author's claimed public-design failures (e.g. the datasheet 1 uH/47 uF design failing R4) to confirm the metric discriminates; confirm the behavioural inductor matches a flux-based implementation.

Evidence status: Draft-only input. fixed_params.json content is supplied text (stated specification, not inspected on disk). The reference outline, budget-fit claims, public-design failure claims, and the mechanism_survival masking claim are unverified author claims; no simulation output, passing design, or runtime measurement is supplied or inspected. Checkable in principle per tools named above; implemented and validated coverage is zero at this stage.

Checks before full-task readiness: (1) simulate a reference design across the full corner set and record worst-corner residual to calibrate 4.0 mV; (2) reproduce one claimed public-design failure to show the metric discriminates; (3) demonstrate ngspice convergence and measure runtime for one full sweep (150+ transient runs at 2.4 ms) plus timestep-sensitivity of the residual at the 2% tolerance; (4) confirm the behavioural L(i) implementation agrees with the stated law; (5) freeze the ESR/C/Isat override convention and design.json schema.

tasks.brief:
We are adding a programmable-gain transconductance front end to a 3-channel battery-powered bridge sensing board. It turns a small differential voltage into an output current feeding a switched-capacitor integrator. Gain changes and channel enable pulses must settle without the bias landing in a wrong state, and gm must stay on target across process, supply and temperature.

Fixed interfaces: supply VDD 1.62 to 1.98 V (1.8 V nominal); inputs inp and inm with common mode 0.9 V +/-0.1 V and differential signal +/-50 mV small-signal, up to +/-400 mV in overload; output node out loaded by the subcircuit in /app/input_assets/load.cir (2 pF behind 10 kohm to a 0.9 V sink; output current is the current into that load). Logic inputs: en (0/1.8 V, 100 ns edges) and gsel (0 = gain A, 1 = gain B). Only the devices in /app/input_assets/mosmodel.lib and ideal resistors and capacitors may be used. Temperature -40 to 125 C. Process corners are defined in the library file; any point inside the stated ranges may be tested.

Requirements:
1. Small-signal gm (output current per differential input volt, at 0.9 V common mode) within +/-4 % of 400 uS for gain A and 100 uS for gain B, at every corner and every combination of supply and temperature in range.
2. Total supply current <= 120 uA at every corner and gain code, enabled.
3. Total gate area W*L summed over all MOS devices <= 400 um^2, minimum length 0.18 um.
4. Power-up from rest (all nodes 0 V, supply ramping 0 to VDD in 50 us): gm within the requirement 1 tolerance within 20 us after the ramp ends.
5. Warm start: supply up, en low for 1 us then high, with internal nodes left at any voltages between 0 and VDD: final supply current within 1 % of the power-up-from-rest value, and gm back within tolerance within 20 us of en rising.
6. Gain switch A to B and B to A with a full-scale (50 mV) input: output current settles to within 1 % of its final value within 5 us, overshoot <= 5 % of the step.
7. Overload: input at +/-400 mV for 2 us, then small signal: output current within 1 % of its small-signal value within 10 us.
8. Robustness: requirements 1, 4 and 5 must still hold with the threshold of any single device shifted by 5 mV in either direction and supply shifted by 2 %.
9. Bias-loop damping: the ring-down of the node you declare in design.json as "loop_node" after a 20 mV supply step (defined in the handbook) must have damping ratio >= 0.45 at every corner.
10. Settled output current must change by less than 0.5 % when the transient time resolution is made twice as fine.

Deliverables in /app/output/: design.cir, a netlist of the stage (subcircuit named gmstage with ports vdd gnd inp inm out en gsel) using the supplied models; design.json with fields "devices" (list of name, W_um, L_um), "gain_codes" (gsel value to nominal gm in uS) and "loop_node" (name of a node inside gmstage that is the bias-loop node).
tasks.handbook:
Model description: mosmodel.lib holds plain SPICE level-1 square-law MOS cards (no subthreshold conduction is modelled; below threshold the current is essentially zero). Temperature behaviour is set explicitly on the cards: tnom=27 C, threshold tc via TCV (NMOS -1.0 mV/K, PMOS +1.0 mV/K on the threshold magnitude) and mobility via UTE=-1.5. Corners: slow = |vto|+30 mV and kp x0.9, fast = |vto|-30 mV and kp x1.1, typ = nominal. Continuous deltas in between may be tested. Typical nominal values: Vth about 0.45 V (N), 0.48 V (P); kp 300 uA/V^2 (N), 100 uA/V^2 (P). Gate capacitance is on the order of 8 fF/um^2. Resistors and capacitors are ideal and not counted in area.

Measurement definitions: gm is output current per differential input volt, with out held at the 0.9 V sink, from a 1 to 5 mV differential step or low-frequency AC. Settling time runs from the event edge to the last time the output leaves the +/-1 % band around its final value. Overshoot is relative to the total step. Supply current is the average DC current from VDD. Settled-state and gm checks use small-signal input 1 to 5 mV.

Ring-down definition (requirement 9): with the stage enabled and settled at gain A, inputs at 0.9 V common mode and zero differential, VDD is stepped by +20 mV in 100 ns and the voltage of the declared loop_node is recorded. The node should be the loop node that sets the output current (for example the bias or tail-control node); the declared node must be a node that exists in design.cir inside gmstage and must not be vdd, gnd or a port. Take the deviation from its final value; successive peaks of alternating sign give the log decrement delta = ln(peak1/peak3) per full cycle, zeta = delta/sqrt(4 pi^2 + delta^2). If fewer than two peaks of opposite sign appear (monotonic response within 5 % of the first excursion) the response counts as zeta >= 0.45. The check is repeated at gain B and at each corner.

Practice notes: bias loops with positive feedback have a stable zero-current state, so a transient from rest and one from arbitrary stored voltages can differ. In strong inversion gm scales with sqrt(mobility*W/L*Id); source degeneration makes gm approach 1/R. Typical supply split for a 120 uA stage: bias 20 to 40 uA, core 60 to 90 uA.
tasks.review:
### 02 · Programmable-gm front end with start-state-independent bias — advance, rank 8

Design decision as written: yes — "We are adding a programmable-gain transconductance front end to a 3-channel battery-powered bridge sensing board... Gain changes and channel enable pulses must settle without the bias landing in a wrong state, and gm must stay on target across process, supply and temperature."

Forge task: Design and size the subcircuit gmstage (vdd gnd inp inm out en gsel) in SPICE using only the supplied MOS models plus ideal R and C, such that gm is 400 uS (gain A) and 100 uS (gain B) within +/-4 % across corners, VDD 1.62-1.98 V and -40 to 125 C, supply current <= 120 uA, total MOS gate area <= 400 um^2, the bias settles to the same state from rest and from arbitrary stored node voltages within 20 us, gain switches settle within 5 us with <= 5 % overshoot, overload recovers within 10 us, the declared bias loop node rings down with zeta >= 0.45, and results are timestep-refinement stable.

Why it fits:
• It asks for a designed artifact (a netlist plus a device table and a declared loop node), not an analysis of a fixed system; the agent chooses topology, sizing, degeneration, startup and compensation.
• The decision is genuinely coupled: constant-gm/deg-referenced bias gives gm accuracy over PVT, but the positive-feedback bias loop has a zero-current basin (start-state dependence), so startup strength trades against the 120 uA current budget, loop damping (zeta >= 0.45) trades against 5 us gain-switch settling and 10 us overload recovery, and all of it is squeezed into 400 um^2 of gate area with L >= 0.18 um.
• Every requirement is expressible as scripted DC, AC or transient checks in ngspice plus Python post-processing and netlist parsing.

What stops it:
• Structural: nothing blocking. The task is a design decision, bounded, and simulable in principle.
• Unresolved feasibility risks: (a) warm-start runs apply .ic voltages on internal nodes — ngspice may fail to converge, and a numerical failure is not evidence of a bistable bias state, so the grader needs a defined policy for convergence failure vs. genuine wrong-state settling; (b) no passing reference netlist exists yet — the author states "Thresholds are provisional until a passing reference is simulated", which is an author claim, not evidence; (c) G1 (27 grid + 20 held-out points), G3 (10 undisclosed seeds x corner subset), G5 (each device singly shifted both signs), G6 (both gains x corners) and G7 imply hundreds of ngspice runs; single-run circuit size makes this plausible but the runtime is unmeasured.

How to check it:
• ngspice: DC/small-signal or 1-5 mV differential-step transient at 0.9 V common mode into the load subcircuit to extract gm per gain code over the corner grid and held-out points (G1), average VDD current (G2 requirement), 50 us supply ramp transient from rest and .ic warm-start transients with en low 1 us (G3), gain-switch and +/-400 mV overload transients with 1 % band settling and overshoot extracted in Python (G4), the same rerun with per-device Vth shifts of +/-5 mV and 2 % supply shift (G5), a +20 mV VDD step in 100 ns with the declared loop_node waveform post-processed by the handbook log-decrement rule for zeta (G6), and the settled-state rerun at half the baseline step (G7).
• Python: parse design.cir and design.json, verify MOS device list consistency, W*L sum <= 400 um^2, L >= 0.18 um, loop_node exists inside gmstage and is not a port or supply rail.
• What a simulation would get wrong: see simulation gaps.

Simulation gaps:
• The supplied level-1 cards model no subthreshold conduction, so near-zero bias states are idealised; real devices leak subthreshold, which changes both the zero-current basin and warm-start recovery. Start-state behaviour is therefore optimistic or pessimistic in ways the model cannot show.
• Ideal resistors and capacitors are stated to be uncounted in area and have no tolerance or temperature coefficient, so gm ≈ 1/R_deg stability across temperature is overstated relative to a real board.
• No mismatch model beyond the single-device +/-5 mV Vth shift, no 1/f or thermal noise, no offset check, no package or board parasitics; the SC integrator is a 10 kohm / 2 pF Thevenin-equivalent load, not the real switched-capacitor waveform.
• Level-1 square-law accuracy for a 0.18 um device class is limited; lambda, gamma and the given TCV/UTE behaviour are approximations. Confirm that ngspice level-1 TCV and UTE reproduce the stated temperature drift (that is a model-consistency check, not validation).
• The zeta extraction assumes an approximately linear second-order ring-down; peak detection and the "fewer than two opposite-sign peaks counts as pass" rule are timestep- and window-sensitive, and a non-converged transient can masquerade as a start-state-dependent wrong basin.

Why frontier models fail:
• The requirements are coupled, not independent: meeting gm +/-4 % across PVT pushes toward a resistor-referenced degenerated loop, whose positive feedback has a stable zero-current state; forcing the correct state consumes current (R2), startup devices load the loop and erode damping (R9), and loop compensation slows gain switching (R6) and overload recovery (R7) while the gate area budget (R3) limits how many helper devices can be added.
• The discriminating requirements (R5 arbitrary stored states with undisclosed seeds, R8 single-device threshold shifts, R9 damping at corners) are exactly the ones a design validated only from a rest-start power-up and timestep halving will miss. That is a hypothesis about model failure, not a measured result.

Real-world risks:
• Real degeneration resistors have tolerance and temperature coefficient, so achieved gm accuracy will exceed the simulated +/-4 %; a real board needs trimming or a better reference.
• Level-1 MOS fidelity, unmodelled subthreshold behaviour, unmodelled mismatch and parasitics mean a design that passes the checker is plausible to work but not demonstrated to work on silicon.
• The battery-powered system's supply ramp, ripple and the 3-channel loading are outside this single-stage scope.

Milestones (if too big): not required at this stage; if runtime measurements show the sweep exceeds one run, split into (1) static gm/current/area target matching over PVT, (2) start-state and enable behaviour, (3) transient behaviour (gain switch, overload) and loop damping, each with its own netlist start state and grader.

What to change (reshape): none — advance as written.

Numbers to supply next:
• Missing specification (not verification): warm-start seed policy — how many seeds, which nodes receive .ic values and their distribution, e.g. 10 seeds, every node inside gmstage drawn uniformly from 0 to VDD, and whether convergence failure counts as a fail.
• Missing specification: R10 baseline transient time step and integrator settings, e.g. max step 5 ns with trap/Gear setting fixed, refined run at 2.5 ns.
• Missing specification: gm measurement stimulus and window, e.g. 2 mV differential step at 0.9 V common mode, output current averaged from 10 us to 20 us after the edge; and the definition of the +20 mV supply step rise time (100 ns is stated — confirm it applies to G6 only).
• Interface: confirm the provided assets exist and match the embedded text — /app/input_assets/mosmodel.lib and /app/input_assets/load.cir are named dependencies, not inspected files. Specify the checker's testbench: whether it instantiates gmstage and .subckt scload with sink at 0.9 V, the top-level node names, and the raw/measure output format the checker reads.
• Output schema (already drafted, keep): design.cir with subcircuit gmstage (vdd gnd inp inm out en gsel); design.json with devices [{name, W_um, L_um}], gain_codes {"0": gm_uS, "1": gm_uS}, loop_node string.
• Handbook data (mostly supplied): keep the level-1 card values (vto 0.45/-0.48 V, kp 300u/100u, TCV -1/+1 mV/K, UTE -1.5), corner definition (|vto| +/-30 mV, kp x0.9/1.1, continuous deltas), supply ramp shape (linear 0 to VDD in 50 us), and ideal R/C not counted in area.
• Verification still needed before full-task readiness: demonstrate one reference netlist that passes all of R1-R10 (the author's reference outline is a proposed solution with provisional thresholds, not a passing design); reproduce at least one claimed public-design failure on R5/R9 to confirm the catching rows discriminate; measure ngspice runtime and convergence rate for .ic transients and the full grid-plus-seeds-plus-shift sweep; confirm ngspice level-1 TCV/UTE behaviour matches the handbook temperature claims.

Evidence status: draft-only input. The instruction, requirements, load.cir and mosmodel.lib text, grader plan and reference outline are author-supplied text; no filesystem inspection or simulation has been performed. The reference outline is a proposed solution and explicitly not validated ("Thresholds are provisional until a passing reference is simulated", author claim). Public-design failure claims and the mechanism-survival narrative are author claims, unverified. The stated grid (27 points) plus held-out points, seeds and per-device shifts implies a large but unmeasured simulation count; no runtime evidence exists.

Checks before full-task readiness: (1) verify /app/input_assets/load.cir and mosmodel.lib exist and match the embedded text; (2) produce and simulate a passing reference design across all grader paths; (3) measure ngspice wall time and convergence for the warm-start .ic runs and define the convergence-failure policy; (4) reproduce a failing baseline for R5, R8 and R9 to show the checks discriminate; (5) confirm level-1 TCV/UTE in ngspice gives the stated drift; (6) fix the R10 step baseline and the R5 seed policy in the task text.

tasks.brief:
We are building a bridge-sensor data-acquisition board and need the front-end block to meet the datasheet numbers below at the connector. The cable can pick up a 10 V transient and the board is power-cycled daily, so the block has to come up and recover the same way every time.

Block: differential input IN_P/IN_N, single-ended output OUT referred to GND, rails VCC = +5 V and VEE = -5 V, load on OUT 10 kohm in parallel with 100 pF. Sensor: two 175 ohm legs (350 ohm differential) joined at a midpoint that is connected to GND; one leg goes to IN_P, the other to IN_N. The sensor signal is 0 to 20 mV differential, DC to 1 kHz. Overload pulse: a voltage source of 10 V, 100 us width, 10 ns edges, positive polarity, inserted in series with the IN_P leg (between the 175 ohm resistor and IN_P). Build the block from the amplifier macro LNA and the clamp diode model DCLAMP in /app/input_assets/lna.lib (at most three LNA instances, noise data in the file header), plus resistors, capacitors (no inductors) and DCLAMP diodes. No other active parts.

Spread: resistors 1 %, capacitors 5 % plus a further +/-3 % drift over temperature, temperature 0 to 70 C, each sensor leg resistance +/-10 %. Every requirement below must hold for every combination inside these ranges, including combinations not named here. Differential gain means OUT / (V(IN_P) - V(IN_N)).

Requirements:
R1. Gain at 100 Hz between 92 and 108 V/V.
R2. Gain at 1 kHz at least -0.5 dB relative to the gain at 100 Hz; gain at 100 kHz at most -66 dB relative to the gain at 100 Hz.
R3. Input-referred rms noise, 1 Hz to 1 kHz, sensor thermal noise included, at 27 C with nominal values: at most 215 nV.
R4. Same noise at any combination of the spread ranges, including 70 C: at most 240 nV.
R5. Power-up with the rails ramping from 0 to +/-5 V in 1 ms, all capacitor voltages initially zero, 10 mV DC differential at the input: OUT within 50 uV of its final value from 20 ms to 40 ms.
R6. Same power-up from any initial capacitor voltages between -4 V and +4 V: same 50 uV limit, and final value within 50 uV of the R5 final value.
R7. Overload: the 10 V, 100 us pulse, applied at any instant after settling: OUT within 50 uV of its pre-pulse value from 5 ms to 20 ms after the pulse starts.
R8. Peak-to-peak ripple on OUT from 15 ms to 20 ms after the pulse starts at most 20 uV.
R9. During the overload, peak current in any DCLAMP diode at most 12 mA and peak current into any LNA input pin at most 2 mA.
R10. Average current drawn from VCC at 10 mV input at most 3 mA.
R11. The OUT values judged in R5 to R7 must be numerically converged: they change by at most 10 uV when the numerical resolution of the time-domain analysis is made four times finer.

Deliverable: /app/output/frontend.cir, a SPICE subcircuit named FRONTEND with ports IN_P IN_N OUT VCC VEE GND, containing only the subcircuit definition. Use literal numeric values (no parameters, no initial-condition statements) and element names starting with R, C, D or X.
tasks.handbook:
Handbook (reference data).

Thermal noise: voltage density sqrt(4kTR), k = 1.38e-23 J/K, T in kelvin (27 C = 300 K, 70 C = 343 K). A 1 kohm resistor gives about 4.1 nV/rtHz at 300 K. Uncorrelated noise adds as power. A noise source with white density e_w and 1/f corner f_c has density squared e_w^2 (1 + f_c/f); over f1 to f2 the integral is e_w^2 [(f2 - f1) + f_c ln(f2/f1)].

Input-referred noise convention: the total output noise density from all sources (resistor thermal noise, amplifier voltage noise, amplifier current noise acting on the local impedance) is divided by the magnitude of the differential signal gain at each frequency and integrated from 1 Hz to 1 kHz. The sensor's 350 ohm differential resistance is included as a noisy resistor at the sensor temperature. Series resistance at an amplifier input adds thermal noise and converts current noise to voltage noise.

Amplifier macro (full text in lna.lib): open-loop DC gain 120 dB, gain-bandwidth 8 MHz (dominant pole near 8 Hz), input voltage noise 4 nV/rtHz white with 1/f corner 20 Hz, input current noise 0.4 pA/rtHz white at each input, output swing +/-4 V, 50 ohm output resistance, quiescent current 1 mA per instance, internal node clamped near +/-6 V to avoid unphysical windup. Noise is represented by AC sources VEN (series with the + input), IIP and IIN that are set to unit amplitude and weighted by these densities when noise is evaluated; they are zero in signal analyses. The input pins are INP and INN; the current into each pin is the current through sense sources VSP and VSN.

Clamp diode DCLAMP: IS = 1e-14 A, N = 1, RS = 2 ohm, CJO = 2 pF; forward drop about 0.6 V at a few mA, conducting from about 0.55 V. A diode from an input node to a rail clamps that node about one drop beyond the rail.

Sensor and overload convention: the sensor midpoint is at GND. The sensor signal for settling and recovery runs is a 10 mV DC differential level, split symmetrically about the midpoint. The pulse is a 10 V, 100 us wide, 10 ns edge voltage step source in series with the IN_P leg, so IN_P is driven toward +10 V through the 175 ohm leg and any series input resistance, with the pulse referenced to GND through the midpoint. Power-up: VCC and VEE ramp linearly from 0 over 1 ms.

Tolerance convention: each resistor and capacitor value is scaled by a factor inside its tolerance band; capacitor drift is a further multiplicative factor within +/-3 % that applies to all capacitors of the design together or separately. The resistance of each sensor leg scales within +/-10 %.

Settling: a response is settled when its deviation from its own final value stays inside the stated band for the whole stated interval. Lightly damped second-order sections have a decay time constant of 2Q/omega0; a pair of poles with Q above about 2 can ring for many milliseconds at kilohertz corner frequencies. Capacitor corner shifts of several percent move the corner of a second-order section by about half that percentage and can alter Q when the two capacitors differ.

Typical practice: a difference amplifier with equal input resistors R1 and feedback resistors R2 has differential gain R2/(R1 + R_leg) for a source leg resistance R_leg and loads the sensor, so source tolerance appears as gain tolerance. Active two-pole low-pass sections come in several standard realisations. Transient simulations may start from user-specified capacitor voltages; time-step convergence is usually checked by comparing runs at dt and dt/4.
tasks.review:
### 08 · Protected bridge-sensor front end — advance, rank 8

Design decision as written: yes — "Build the block from the amplifier macro LNA and the clamp diode model DCLAMP ... plus resistors, capacitors (no inductors) and DCLAMP diodes"; deliverable is "/app/output/frontend.cir, a SPICE subcircuit named FRONTEND".

Forge task: Design a two- to three-amplifier bridge front end (topology and literal R/C values, rail clamping) that delivers 92–108 V/V at 100 Hz with the specified 1 kHz/100 kHz shape, ≤215/≤240 nV input-referred noise, start-state-independent settling within 50 µV, 5 ms overload recovery from a 10 V/100 µs pulse with ≤12 mA diode / ≤2 mA pin peak currents, ≤3 mA VCC current, all corners of ±1 % R, ±5 %±3 % C, ±10 % sensor legs, 0–70 °C, and dt-converged judged values — emitted as one ngspice subcircuit.

Why it fits:
• The deliverable is a component-value and topology decision, not a report or a simulation of a fixed system.
• Every requirement row has a named headless check: AC sweeps (R1, R2), AC-transfer-weighted noise integration in numpy (R3, R4), ngspice transient with 1 ms rail ramp and checker-injected .ic (R5, R6, R10), pulsed transient with current probes (R7, R8, R9), paired dt / dt/4 runs (R11), netlist parse (G6).
• The physics that matters (op-amp macro poles, diode clamping, RC/Q of the low-pass section, thermal and 1/f noise, resistor-loading gain tolerance) is exactly what the stated tools model.
• The requirement set is genuinely coupled: the droop and −66 dB rows fix the low-pass corner within roughly ±8 %, overload current sets a minimum series resistance, and the noise budget caps it — a real packaging/trade-off problem.

What stops it:
• Structural: none — the task is a design decision and all rows are checkable in principle with ngspice + numpy.
• Unresolved feasibility risks (not missing numbers): (a) runtime — G3/G4/G5 ask for many 60–80 ms transients over tolerance interiors and two time steps; with 10 ns pulse edges this could exceed the agent's own verification budget within a 2 h run; (b) ngspice robustness of checker-injected .ic on arbitrary capacitor states and of 10 ns edges driving a clamped input; (c) R11's reference time step is undefined, so "four times finer" is not yet reproducible; (d) R6 wording leaves open whether LNA-internal capacitors are part of the precharge set; (e) the noise limit sits close to the handbook-derived floor — rough arithmetic on the supplied densities gives order 170–190 nV at 27 °C nominal with ~300 Ω per leg and gain ~100, consistent with the author's unverified 185–200 nV claim but with little margin at 70 °C corners.

How to check it:
• ngspice (AC): differential gain magnitude at 100 Hz, 1 kHz, 100 kHz vs the 100 Hz reference, at nominal, grouped corners and seeded random interior samples.
• ngspice (AC) + numpy: transfer functions from each LNA's VEN/IIP/IIN (unit amplitude) and resistor thermal noise to OUT, divided by differential gain squared, integrated 1 Hz–1 kHz with the stated white + 1/f formula; 27 °C nominal and 70 °C/tolerance interiors.
• ngspice (transient): 0–60 ms run with 1 ms rail ramp, 10 mV DC input, zero and random .ic capacitor states; deviation from mean(55–60 ms) final value over 20–40 ms, cross-start final-value difference, mean VCC current 40–60 ms.
• ngspice (transient): 10 V/100 µs, 10 ns-edge PWL in series with the IN_P leg at checker-chosen instants; OUT deviation 5–20 ms, p–p 15–20 ms, diode and VSP/VSN peak currents.
• ngspice (transient, repeated) at max step dt and dt/4 for R11; Python netlist parse for element/port constraints.

Simulation gaps:
• The behavioural LNA macro (tanh swing limiter, clamp B-source, 50 Ω output, fixed 19.9 pF internal pole) is a model, not silicon: no input capacitance, no PSRR/CMRR, no supply-dependent bias, no diode self-heating, no PCB parasitics, so real EMI on the cable and actual clamp energy are not represented.
• The noise route is AC-transfer weighting, not a native .noise run; agreement between the two must be demonstrated, and 1/f noise of the macro is applied externally rather than by the model itself.
• Convergence/accuracy at 10 ns edges and near-diode conduction, and the numerical noise floor of the 50 µV judgments (relative to R11's 10 µV allowance), are untested here.
• Corners-plus-random sampling cannot prove all-combinations compliance; interior worst cases (e.g. Q and corner drifting together) may be missed.

Why frontier models fail:
• Plausible, not demonstrated: the window is narrow and multi-constraint — a first-order filter cannot meet both R2 rows, a high-Q section fails R7/R8, AC coupling fails R5/R6 and 1/f noise, large input resistors fail R4, small ones fail R9, three-amplifier instrumentation topologies fail R10. Correctly trading gain tolerance (±10 % legs enter the gain), noise, clamp current and settling time through a whole power-up and overload cycle, and then converging transient numerics, is real engineering reasoning rather than pattern completion.

Real-world risks:
• Model-to-hardware gaps above; plus cable-transient common-mode coupling is only represented as a series differential pulse, real clamps need surge/energy consideration beyond 12 mA peak, resistor tolerance is treated as independent scaling (real parts correlate), and the LNA macro's unspecified input capacitance could change clamp/settling behaviour in a build.

Milestones (if too big): Not required if checker sweep runtimes are measured first; if they are not, split as (1) gain/noise stage design with G1/G2 graders and (2) protection plus settling/recovery with G3–G5 graders, each with its own starting testbench and reference netlist.

What to change (reshape): None — pin down the items under "Numbers to supply next"; these are specification fill-ins, not a change of device or core decision.

Numbers to supply next:
  • Requirement: R11 time-step basis — e.g. max step dt = 2 µs in G3/G4 transient runs, compared against dt = 0.5 µs; state that pulse edges are ideal 10 ns PWL in the checker testbench.
  • Requirement: R6 precharge scope — e.g. .ic applied only to capacitors declared inside frontend.cir, LNA-internal C1 left at model default; 12 random precharge vectors within ±4 V.
  • Requirement: temperature and drift coverage for R5–R8 — e.g. judged at 27 °C nominal plus 4 grouped corners at 0 °C and 70 °C, or full interior sampling; state explicitly.
  • Requirement: sample counts and seeds — e.g. 60 random interior samples for G1/G2, 13 starts × 20 spread samples for G3, 30 pulse instants × 20 spread samples for G4, fixed seed, plus an upper bound on total checker CPU (e.g. 4 h) so the agent can mirror it.
  • Interface: inputs /app/input_assets/lna.lib and the checker-built testbench (two 175 Ω legs at GND midpoint, 10 kΩ ‖ 100 pF load, ±5 V rails); output /app/output/frontend.cir containing only '.subckt FRONTEND IN_P IN_N OUT VCC VEE GND ... .ends'; state the exact metric extraction (e.g. final value = mean OUT over 55–60 ms).
  • Handbook data: already supplied (k = 1.38e-23, white + 1/f integral, LNA and DCLAMP parameters, tolerance convention). Add: whether arbitrary literal values are allowed or an E-series grid applies (e.g. E24 for R), and the max element count if any.
  • Verification still needed before full-task readiness: reproduce at least one passing design in ngspice and record the judged values; measure runtime of the G4/G5 sweeps at the stated dt; confirm ngspice accepts .ic on the design's capacitor nodes and converges the 10 ns pulse; cross-check the numpy noise combination against a native ngspice .noise run at nominal; confirm the 70 °C corner noise stays under 240 nV in an actual run, not just handbook arithmetic.

Evidence status: draft-only input. The reference outline, the 185–200 nV / 2.4 mA / 9 mA estimates, the listed public-design failures and the mechanism-survival narrative are author claims, unverified; no simulation output, netlist artifact or runtime measurement has been inspected. Handbook arithmetic above is my engineering inference, not measured evidence. lna.lib text is supplied content establishing the model text, not physical fidelity.
