tasks.brief:
I need a 3.3 V input block for a sensor-board radio that transmits in bursts. It runs from an adapter-plus-battery rail that is soft and noisy. We have had field resets from rails that ring or settle into a different pattern depending on how the board was powered up, so the numbers below must hold from any starting charge state.

Fixed: the source is 4.5 to 5.5 V open-circuit behind 1.0 ohm. The load is an ideal current sink on vout, either constant at 20 to 600 mA, or a burst between 50 and 600 mA (30% duty, 1 us edges, burst rate anywhere in 8 to 14 kHz). Use only the parts in components.json and models.lib. Capacitors vary by +/-10% and inductors by +/-15%, in any combination. Use at most 25 parts and 150 mm2. The ports are vin, vout, gnd. The 'rail signal' is vout low-passed at 200 kHz, zero-phase. Every requirement below holds over the whole source range, burst-rate range and tolerance range.

Requirements:
R1: raw vout stays within 3.201 to 3.399 V at constant 20 mA and at constant 600 mA.
R2: cold start (all capacitor voltages and inductor currents zero, source ramped to its value in 1 ms, burst load running from t=0): the rail signal is inside 3.3 V +/-3% and stays there from at most 5 ms after the ramp starts.
R3: cold start: rail signal peak at most 3.45 V.
R4: warm restart, with capacitor voltages anywhere in 0 to 3.6 V and inductor currents anywhere in 0 to 1 A, otherwise as R2: the rail signal is inside the window from at most 8 ms.
R5: warm restart: over the last burst period before 20 ms, the rail signal differs from the cold-start run (same burst rate, source and tolerances) by at most 5 mV at any instant.
R6: burst load: raw vout ripple at most 60 mV pk-pk over the burst periods between 15 and 20 ms.
R7: burst load: |rail(t+Tb) - rail(t)| at most 5 mV for all t between 15 and 20 ms, where Tb is the burst period.
R8: load step 20 to 600 mA in 1 us: raw droop below the pre-step value at most 120 mV.
R9: the same step: the rail signal returns within +/-1% of the pre-step value in at most 100 us and stays inside it for the next 2 ms.
R10: constant 300 mA load, the source falls to 3.8 V in 50 us, holds 2 ms, then recovers in 50 us: raw vout stays at or above 3.135 V throughout.
R11: the same event: from 100 us after recovery ends for 2 ms, the rail signal stays within 40 mV of its pre-dropout value.
R12: a 50 mV pk-pk sine at any frequency from 100 kHz to 1 MHz on the source, 300 mA constant load: the output component at that frequency is at most 5 mV pk-pk.
R13: the burst ripple, the mean rail and the R5 difference each change by at most 2 mV when the time resolution of the evaluation is made twice as fine.
R14: at 5.5 V source and constant 600 mA, average dissipation in any single active device or resistor is at most 0.8 W.
R15: the parts list has at most 25 parts and at most 150 mm2 in total.

Deliver /app/output/design.sp, a SPICE netlist with a .subckt DESIGN vin vout gnd. It may reference only the models.lib subcircuits, resistors and the parts in components.json. Deliver /app/output/parts.json, a JSON list of {ref, class, value} for every instance, with refs equal to the netlist instance names.
tasks.handbook:
Inputs: /app/input_assets/components.json (parts, areas, parameters) and /app/input_assets/models.lib (behavioural subcircuits). Both are fully listed. Ground in models.lib is node 0, and the wrapper ties gnd to node 0. Units are SI. Instance forms are in components.json. Capacitor and inductor parameters must be copied from a table row; c0 and l0 are the nominal values that tolerances scale.

Part models. Capacitor: C_eff = c0/(1+(v/vh)^2), with series ESR and ESL, so charge Q = c0*vh*atan(v/vh). Inductor: L = l0/(1+(i/isat)^2), with series DCR, so flux = l0*isat*atan(i/isat). The model clamps at hard saturation. PASS conducts (v(i)-v(o))*clamp(v(g),0,5)/5/0.08 A. SW is a smooth switch, 0.1 ohm on, threshold 2.5 V. EA is a single-pole amplifier: DC gain 1e5, GBW 5 MHz, output 0 to 5 V through 100 ohm, non-inverting input p. CMP is a comparator with a 0 to 5 V output. OSC is a 0 to 2 V triangle at parameter f. VREF is 1.2 V. DSCH is a Schottky diode (Vf about 0.4 V at 0.5 A). Each part counts once toward the part limit and area, whatever its class. The netlist may not contain other behavioural sources, switches or diodes.

Initial states. Capacitor voltage is imposed on node n2 of each CAP instance relative to its b terminal. An inductor current i0 is imposed as flux on node ph of each IND instance: v(ph) = l0*isat*atan(i0/isat). Source ramps start at t=0. Warm states are drawn independently per element.

Definitions. Rail signal: vout filtered by a zero-phase 2nd-order Butterworth low-pass at 200 kHz. Ripple (R6) uses raw vout. Settled means inside 3.201 to 3.399 V of the rail signal for the rest of the run. Tolerance corners scale each part by a factor inside its band, either all at the extremes or drawn at random. Burst period Tb = 1/burst rate; burst phase starts at t=0 with the load high for the first 30% of each period. Burst rates are sampled across 8 to 14 kHz, not only at the band edges. R12: the pk-pk of the component at the injected frequency is 2 x its Fourier amplitude, taken over an integer number of cycles after 3 ms; the injected frequency may be any value in the band. R13 compares runs with maximum timestep 100 ns and 50 ns. Dissipation is the time average of v*i across the device over one burst period, or over 1 ms for constant loads, after settling.

Practice ranges. Ceramic capacitors lose 20 to 60% of c0 at 3.3 V depending on class (see vh). Capacitor ESL of 0.3 to 2 nH sets the response to 1 us edges. LC resonance is f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C_eff)); inductance and capacitance both move with bias and tolerance. A step in current of 0.58 A delivers charge to the output over a loop response time of 1 to 5 us. Switching frequencies of 50 kHz to 2 MHz are practical with the supplied OSC, and a 1 us burst edge contains energy to about 300 kHz. In the dropout state the source drops 0.3 V at 300 mA. Source resistance of 1.0 ohm drops 0.6 V at 600 mA. Simulation of start-up over 20 ms with 100 ns steps typically takes seconds to minutes per case.
tasks.review:
### 27-27 · Burst-radio 3.3 V rail from any start state — advance, rank 7

Design decision as written: yes — "I need a 3.3 V input block for a sensor-board radio that transmits in bursts... Deliver /app/output/design.sp, a SPICE netlist with a .subckt DESIGN vin vout gnd"; the deliverable is a circuit topology and part selection, not an analysis.

Forge task: Synthesize a 3.3 V input block (buck, LDO, or combination) from the allowed components.json parts and models.lib subcircuits, with chosen damping, compensation and start-up behaviour, meeting R1–R15 on regulation, cold/warm-start settling and convergence, burst ripple, periodicity, load step, dropout, injected-sine rejection, timestep convergence, device dissipation and part/area limits; output a SPICE netlist plus a matching parts list.

Why it fits:
• It asks for a design artifact (netlist + parts.json) whose topology, inductor/capacitor choice, damping branch and compensation are the engineer's decision; every row is a numeric pass/fail a script can compute.
• ngspice can run the wrapped transients headless; scipy can apply the zero-phase 200 kHz Butterworth, compute ripple, periodicity and Fourier amplitude; Python can parse the netlist and sum area (R15).
• The rows are genuinely coupled: damping buys R4/R5/R7/R11/R13 but costs R8 droop, R6 ripple, R14 dissipation and R15 area; a diode buck loses headroom against R10 dropout; fsw trades R7 filtered ripple against R13 timestep convergence (100 ns max step is only ~10 points per 500 kHz cycle, ~5 per 2 MHz cycle).
• Held-out burst rates (8.6–13.4 kHz), source voltages, tolerance draws and warm states reward a design that is robustly contractive, not one tuned to a single nominal run.

What stops it:
• Structural objection: none — this is design synthesis with scripted checking, not analysis or measurement.
• Unresolved feasibility risks: (a) models.lib is supplied text only and has not been shown to run: CAP uses `ddt()` inside a behavioural source and IND uses `tan()` with `max/min` clamping, both non-smooth; parsing and convergence, especially from imposed warm states on CAP n2 / IND ph nodes, must be demonstrated in the pinned ngspice version. (b) Runtime arithmetic does not yet establish a two-hour fit: one 25 ms run at max step 100 ns is ≥2.5e5 timepoints, and the handbook's "seconds to minutes per case" is an author claim; 30–50 corner cases at 1–3 minutes is 30–150 minutes of simulation alone, before design and debugging. (c) No passing reference design has been simulated (reference_outline is explicitly "not yet run"), so R5's 5 mV warm-vs-cold match and R7's 5 mV periodicity against non-commensurate switching ripple are plausible, not demonstrated: after a 200 kHz 2nd-order LPF, residual ripple must be only a few mV, which pushes fsw up and R13 down. (d) R12 (≤5 mV pk-pk at 1 MHz from a 50 mV pk-pk source through 1 Ω) is a demanding PSRR target where the EA loop is out of band and ESL dominates the ceramics. (e) The claimed failures of the listed public designs are author hypotheses, unverified.

How to check it:
• ngspice: transient runs with verifier-built source, 1 Ω source resistance, constant and burst current sinks, initial states imposed on CAP n2 and IND ph nodes, for R1–R11 and R14; Fourier extraction over integer cycles after 3 ms for R12.
• scipy: zero-phase 2nd-order Butterworth at 200 kHz for the rail signal, pk-pk and |rail(t+Tb)-rail(t)| metrics, warm-vs-cold difference, and the 100 ns vs 50 ns comparison for R13.
• Python: parse design.sp/parts.json, check instance refs, table-row parameters (0.1%), resistor range, part count and summed area for R15.

Simulation gaps:
• Behavioural models only: no layout parasitics, thermal model, core loss, temperature or ageing, real ESR/ESL drift, EMI, or a real radio load (the load is an ideal current sink); PASS and SW are idealized conductances and EA is a single pole, so loop stability margins are inferred, not measured.
• The 200 kHz filtered rail deliberately hides switching ripple, so a design can pass R2–R5/R7/R9/R11 and still put millivolts of raw ripple at the radio.
• R13 measures solver convergence, not physical accuracy; a design can agree at 100 ns and 50 ns yet be wrong versus finer integration or hardware. Tolerance is one scalar per part, not a real distribution.

Why frontier models fail: hypothesis, untested — the trap is self-consistent simulation at nominal values, one burst rate and zero initial states, which plausibly shows all rows passing while verifier-held warm states, off-nominal burst rates and derated LC corners reveal slow ringing, distinct periodic orbits and subharmonic content (R4/R5/R7/R11), and limit-cycle jitter breaks R13; fixing these costs damping, which collides with R6/R8/R14/R15.

Real-world risks: no loop-gain/stability verification; dropout behaviour of a diode buck near D≈0.95 at Vin=3.8 V; 0.8 W per device leaves little thermal margin in a small board block; real startup into a radio's dynamic impedance may differ from an ideal sink; component derating and lifetime unmodelled.

Milestones (if measured runtime exceeds one run):
1. Steady-state and step block (R1, R6, R8, R9, R14, R15): supplied netlist graded on constant loads, burst ripple, load step, dissipation and area.
2. Start-state robustness (R2–R5, R7): cold/warm sweeps at held-out burst rates, source voltages and tolerance corners.
3. Dropout, injection and convergence (R10–R13): source dropout profile, 100 kHz–1 MHz injection, and 100 ns vs 50 ns comparison.
Each milestone would need its own starting files, grader and a reference design.

What to change (reshape): • Nothing structural at Stage 1; pinning down runtime, corner counts and the wrapper template is specification work, not a reshape. • If measured per-case runtimes make the full sweep exceed roughly two hours, split into the three milestones above rather than trimming requirements.

• Interface: exact wrapper template — source ramp subcircuit, 1 Ω series resistance, burst load definition (30% duty, 1 µs edges, phase 0 at t=0), .ic syntax for CAP n2 and IND ph, and the transient output schema (e.g., ASCII columns time, v(vout) at ≤100 ns spacing).

• Handbook data: confirmed support in the pinned ngspice build for `ddt()` in B-sources and the clamped `tan()` IND model, plus a smoke-test bench showing models.lib parses and a trivial circuit converges from imposed warm states.

Never widen a limit to obtain a passing design.

tasks.brief:
We are adding a pluggable accessory module to a 12 V backplane and need the power-entry stage designed. The module hot-plugs onto a bus with a lightly damped cable, and its downstream converter acts as a constant-power load once enabled. The stage must behave the same whether it is plugged in cold, re-plugged with residual charge on the output, or released from a current limit.

Fixed interfaces: the stage is a SPICE subcircuit named ENTRY with ports in this order: VIN VOUT GND VAUX EN. VAUX is an auxiliary rail of 5 to 12 V (use 8 V nominal) and EN is a 0/5 V enable input, high = on. The pass device is the N-channel MOSFET subcircuit PASSFET (pins D G S) in /app/input_assets/models.lib; one or more instances may be used. The op-amp macro OPA_GBW and comparator macro CMP_IDEAL in the same file may be used. Other parts are discrete passives; any sense resistor is 10 to 50 mOhm. Output capacitance 220 uF (ESR 0.03 ohm) is added outside ENTRY at VOUT. Do not include it, the source or the load in your subcircuit.

Source: an ideal DC bus voltage VBUS of 10.8 to 13.2 V behind 0.15 ohm series, 1.2 uH cable inductance and a 100 uF bulk capacitor with 0.05 ohm ESR at the entry-stage side; cable inductance and bulk ESR each vary independently by +/-25 percent. VIN means the ENTRY port VIN node. Load: 18 W constant power, starting 5 ms after EN rises, dropping out below 8 V at VOUT.

Requirements, all with the module enabled at t=0 unless stated. In R3 to R5, the reference voltage is VBUS (the DC source value, not the ringing VIN node), and the time to reach 2 percent is the last instant after which VOUT stays within 2 percent of VBUS (for R5, of its pre-sag value).
R1. Peak current into VIN during cold plug (VOUT initially 0 V): <= 4.0 A, at every bus voltage and tolerance corner.
R2. Energy dissipated in the pass devices, sum over all PASSFET instances of the integral of Vds*Id, cold plug from 0 to 30 ms: <= 0.25 J.
R3. VOUT within 2 percent of VBUS from 12 ms after EN onward, for cold plug.
R4. Warm re-plug with VOUT precharged to any value between 0 and 11 V: same R1 and R3 limits, pass-device energy <= 0.25 J, and VOUT never exceeds VBUS by more than 0.3 V.
R5. Bus sag (VBUS drops by 3 V for 2 ms) applied after the load has started: VOUT is back within 2 percent of its pre-sag value within 5 ms after the sag ends and stays there until 30 ms after the sag ends. Latch-up is defined as VOUT failing this condition, or the load dropping out and not restarting, by 30 ms.
R6. With the load running at steady state, any bus voltage and tolerance corner: peak-to-peak oscillation of VOUT over 20 to 30 ms after EN (and, for the sag case, over 20 to 30 ms after the sag ends) <= 50 mV.
R7. Results must not change materially with simulation resolution: each metric above changes by <= 3 percent of its limit when the time resolution is made two and four times finer.

Deliver /app/output/entry.cir, a SPICE netlist containing the ENTRY subcircuit (it may .include the supplied model file by that path) and nothing else that drives the ports.
tasks.handbook:
Conventions. Input current is the current drawn from the bus source through VIN into ENTRY. Energy is the time integral of drain-source voltage times drain current over the window, summed over all pass devices. Ripple is max minus min of VOUT in the window. The constant-power load is a current source I = P/VOUT, clamped for VOUT below about 1 V to avoid singularity, switched off when VOUT falls below 8 V (0.5 V hysteresis on restart). It presents negative incremental resistance -V^2/P, about -3.6 ohm at 8 V, which destabilises against the source resonance.

Practice. A 1.2 uH / 100 uF source has characteristic impedance near 0.11 ohm and resonance near 14 kHz, damped only by 0.15 + 0.05 ohm. Charging 220 uF to 12 V stores about 16 mJ; a linear pass element charging a capacitor from a fixed supply dissipates about the same energy, plus load-related loss while the load is active. The real energy risk is the load starting while the pass device is still in its linear region, or a stuck partially on state. At 18 W and 8 V the load current is 2.25 A.

Loop practice. Current-limit loops around a MOSFET have a gate pole from gate resistance and Cgs/Cgd, and the output capacitor forms a dominant pole. Integrator or compensation nodes retain state across events, so their value after a limit release or warm plug differs from cold plug.

Models (see models.lib). PASSFET: level-1 MOSFET, Vth 2.5 V, effective Kp*W/L about 0.05 to 0.1 A/V^2 (a few amps need roughly 4.5 to 6 V gate drive), Rds(on) about 20 mOhm at 10 V, Cgs 900 pF, Cgd 120 pF extra. OPA_GBW: single pole at 20 Hz, open-loop gain 100 dB, so GBW 2 MHz, output limited to the supply rails, input offset 1 mV. CMP_IDEAL: output swings between VEE and VCC, about 50 ns delay.

Simulation. Start states are set with initial conditions on VOUT; the source bulk capacitor starts charged to the bus voltage. 4 A through 50 mOhm is 0.2 V, through 10 mOhm 40 mV, comparable to the op-amp offset.
tasks.review:
### 16-hotplug-entry-stage-12v-cpl · Hot-plug 12 V power-entry stage — advance, rank 7

Design decision as written: yes — "we need the power-entry stage designed", with design freedom "parameter selection" and a topology left open ("any topology accepted" in G1).

Forge task: Design the topology and component values of a hot-plug power-entry circuit delivered as `.subckt ENTRY VIN VOUT GND VAUX EN` (PASSFET / OPA_GBW / CMP_IDEAL macros plus passives), such that the checker's wrapper deck meets inrush (≤4.0 A), pass-device energy (≤0.25 J), 12 ms settling to 2 % of VBUS, warm-plug overshoot (≤0.3 V), 5 ms sag recovery without latch-up, ≤50 mV ripple and ≤3 % metric drift under timestep refinement, at every bus/tolerance corner and precharge state.

Why it fits:
• It is a genuine physical design decision: topology (soft-start ramp, current limit, damping), compensation values, sense resistor value and device counts are the agent's to choose; the output is a netlist a headless simulator drives.
• ngspice can evaluate every requirement without a human: transient runs of the supplied wrapper give peak VIN current, per-PASSFET ∫Vds·Id, band-exit time, overshoot, settling and ripple; corner sweeps and timestep repeats are pure scripting.
• The difficulty is real engineering, not tedium: constant-power load negative incremental resistance (−V²/P ≈ −3.6 Ω at 8 V) against the 1.2 µH / 100 µF source resonance (~14 kHz, Z0 ≈ 0.11 Ω — my arithmetic agrees with the handbook), a gate pole from Cgs/Cgd with a dominant output pole, and compensation-node state that differs between cold plug, warm plug and limit release.
• R4/R5/R6 as specified do discriminate robust designs from designs tuned to one natural start state, which is the mechanism the author intends (author claim, not trial-verified).

What stops it:
• Structural objections: none. The device and the core decision (design the entry stage) are unchanged by any fix below.
• Unresolved feasibility risk 1 (my arithmetic on the supplied model text, not simulated): PASSFET is `LEVEL=1 ... KP=0.08` with `W=1 L=1`, so effective Kp·W/L = 0.08 A/V². That gives Rds(on) ≈ 1/(0.08·(10−2.5)) ≈ 1.7 Ω at Vgs = 10 V and ≈ 0.5 A saturation current at Vgs = 6 V, versus the handbook's "Rds(on) about 20 mOhm at 10 V" and "a few amps need roughly 4.5 to 6 V gate drive". A consistent device would need Kp·W/L ≈ 8 A/V² (e.g. W=100 L=1). With the macro literally as written, holding 18 W at 2 % of 12 V looks infeasible; model and handbook must be reconciled before the task is runnable.
• Unresolved feasibility risk 2: VAUX is a ground-referenced 5–12 V rail while the pass device is a high-side NMOS whose source sits at VOUT ≈ 12 V, so Vgs = VAUX − VOUT ≤ 0 in steady state. The reference outline ("gate ramp is a current-source charged capacitor from VAUX") inherits this. Gate drive above VOUT (bootstrap/charge pump built only from allowed passives) must be explicitly permitted, or the device/placement changed — otherwise no design can pass.
• Unresolved feasibility risk 3: the grader sweep is large (27 corners × ~4 scenarios × 3 timesteps ≈ 300 transients, before held-out precharge draws and offsets). No runtime has been measured; behavioural sources (tanh comparator, clamped CPL) may also force small steps or fail convergence at abrupt events.
• Author claims not corroborated: the public-design failure narratives (RC soft start breaking R1/R2/R4, plain op-amp limiter breaking R6, timer hot-swap controller breaking R5/R4) and the mechanism_survival story are hypotheses in the draft; no run artifacts are supplied.

How to check it:
• ngspice: wrap `/app/output/entry.cir` in the specified source (VBUS, 0.15 Ω, 1.2 µH, 100 µF/0.05 Ω), 220 µF/0.03 Ω output cap and the constant-power load; run cold plug, warm plug (IC on VOUT at 0–11 V), and 3 V/2 ms sag transients at all L/ESR/bus corners.
• ngspice + post-processing: peak VIN current and VOUT band-exit time from saved node voltages/branch currents; ∫Vds·Id per PASSFET instance by hierarchical device saves or behavioural power sources; cross-check energy against input-minus-output-cap-minus-load balance (grader plan's 10 % agreement rule).
• ngspice: repeat each case at max step 1 / 0.5 / 0.25 µs and diff every metric for R7.
• Scripted sweep driver (Python) enumerating the corner grid and held-out draws, with per-case pass/fail JSON for the grader.

Simulation gaps:
• LEVEL=1 MOSFET has no temperature, self-heating, SOA or package inductance; level-1 short-channel behaviour is not a real hot-swap FET.
• The CPL clamp near VOUT ≈ 1 V and the 8 V dropout with 0.5 V hysteresis are behavioural conventions; small changes in their implementation can shift sag-recovery and latch-up outcomes.
• CMP_IDEAL's tanh is smooth but steep (200 V⁻¹); interaction with adaptive stepping is a known source of metric noise — R7 exists because of this, and its own noise floor must be measured.
• Energy integration accuracy depends on saved-point density; the checker must integrate from the simulated waveform, not from a coarse export.
• Nothing in simulation checks PCB layout, thermal design, EMI, connector contact physics, or passive tolerance drift beyond the declared corners.

Why frontier models fail (hypothesis unless trials run):
• The competing loops (gate ramp, current limit, load-enable guard, damping RC) interact; a design can pass cold start at nominal while the compensation node left charged by a warm plug or a limit release re-enters with a different state.
• The constant-power load's negative incremental resistance moves the effective damping and can push the ~14 kHz resonance toward crossover; ripple ≤50 mV at every corner requires damping and loop shaping to be solved together, not sequentially.
• Robustness over L/ESR ±25 %, three bus voltages and arbitrary precharge values is a multidimensional tuning problem where one-at-a-time sweeps lie; plus the R7 convergence requirement punishes designs that only work at one timestep.

Real-world risks:
• A netlist that passes still needs a real pass device with adequate SOA/thermal margin for the ≤0.25 J events and 2.25 A steady state; not checked here.
• Gate-drive headroom and any bootstrap network must exist in hardware (charge-pump/level-shifter reality), and sense-resistor Kelvin layout matters at 10–50 mΩ where a 1 mV op-amp offset is comparable to the sense signal (handbook point, arithmetically consistent: 4 A × 50 mΩ = 0.2 V, 4 A × 10 mΩ = 40 mV).
• Model fidelity gap: a passing design may still ring on a real cable with different parasitics than 1.2 µH / 0.15 Ω / 100 µF.

Milestones (only if the sweep runtime forces a split): 1. Cold-plug entry (R1–R3): netlist plus wrapper; grader checks peak current, energy and settling at corners. 2. Warm plug + sag (R4–R5): same netlist, IC-on-VOUT and sag wrapper; grader checks overshoot, settling, latch-up. 3. Robustness (R6–R7): ripple windows and timestep refinement on the same netlist. Each is standalone with its own wrapper deck and reference netlist; the deliverable file is identical across milestones.

What to change (reshape): • Nothing structural. Keep the device, the ENTRY interface and all seven requirements; only supply the model/interface numbers listed below and reconcile the PASSFET drive strength.

Numbers to supply next:
• Missing spec — PASSFET drive strength: effective Kp·W/L consistent with the handbook, e.g. `W=100 L=1` (≈8 A/V²) so Rds(on) ≈ 20 mΩ at Vgs = 10 V; supply the corrected `models.lib` text and its path.
• Missing spec — gate-drive headroom: maximum Vgs and maximum gate-node voltage relative to VOUT/GND, and whether a bootstrap/charge-pump network built from permitted passives is allowed — e.g. "gate node up to 24 V abs max, Vgs ≤ 20 V, bootstrap from VIN via diode + capacitor permitted".
• Missing spec — permitted parts: whether diodes and inductors count as "discrete passives", and instance budget — e.g. "R, C, small-signal D and one ≤100 µH L allowed; ≤6 PASSFET, ≤2 OPA_GBW, ≤2 CMP_IDEAL".

• Missing spec — passive tolerances for the agent's own parts: e.g. "resistors 1 %, capacitors ±10 % with ESR ≤0.05 Ω, sense resistor 1 % in 10–50 mΩ".
• Missing spec — timing: EN rise time (e.g. 100 ns), exact sag application time(s) (e.g. at t = 20 ms after EN and a second case at t = 6 ms), total simulated time (e.g. 60 ms), and that the load enables 5 ms after EN (already stated).

tasks.brief:
We need a loop-filter design for a narrowband sensor-readout converter. It digitizes a 20 kHz band centred on a 160 kHz carrier (150 to 170 kHz) at a 2.56 MHz clock, and the loop filter is built from at most two resonator stages. It ships without trimming, so the real resonances will sit somewhat off the design values from lot to lot and over temperature, and it has to keep working anyway.

Fixed inputs are in /app/input_assets/input.json (clock, full scale, quantizer, noise numbers, burst and initial-state settings). The loop model that defines the design parameters is in the reference notes. Please deliver /app/output/design.json with these fields: n_res (1 or 2); stages (a list of n_res objects with theta_rad, leak_g, b_x, b_f, c_prev); ff (list of n_res feedforward weights); d_x; c_in_pf; chopping (true or false). c_prev is used only in stage 2.

Requirements (tone 0.5 FS unless stated; SNDR is measured on the output code stream in 150 to 170 kHz):

R1. In-band SNDR lies between 68 and 74 dB for every tone frequency in 150 to 170 kHz, with each stage's resonance angle off nominal by up to +/-1.5%, integrator input gains off by up to +/-5%, effective quantizer gain from 0.8x to 1.25x, extra resonator loss up to 0.5%, and noise amplitude at 1.0x and 1.5x. Measured after settling, on a 32768-sample record.

R2. From zero state and from random initial integrator states up to 0.3 FS, the integrator-state rms over cycles 1500 to 2000 is within 5% of its value over cycles 8000 to 16000. This holds under every R1 condition.

R3. Over 8 consecutive coherent 4096-cycle windows after settling, the output fundamental's phase has a standard deviation of at most 0.5 degrees. The amplitude change between consecutive windows is at most 0.1 dB. This holds under every R1 condition at 1.5x noise.

R4. After a 200-cycle burst of a 1.2 FS in-band tone, the loop returns within 1000 cycles to integrator-state rms within 10% of steady state, in every 100-cycle window thereafter. The SNDR measured later, after 3000 cycles, is within the R1 window.

R5. With the 0.5 FS tone, no more than 0.5% of samples have quantizer input magnitude above full scale, and every integrator state stays below 5 FS. This holds under every R1 condition.

R6. Parameters stay in bounds: theta_rad 0.30 to 0.50; leak_g 0.90 to 1.00; every b_x, b_f, c_prev, ff and d_x magnitude at most 4; c_in_pf 0.5 to 2.0.

No trimming or digital calibration is available.
tasks.handbook:
REFERENCE NOTES (normalized units: full scale FS = 1, equal to fs_volts in input.json).

Nominal loop model. Per clock cycle n, with input x[n] (signal plus noise) and quantizer output y[n]. Stage k has state (u_k, v_k) and updates:
[u_k;v_k][n+1] = g_k * R(theta_k) [u_k;v_k][n] + [1;0] * ( b_x_k*x[n] - b_f_k*y[n] + c_k*u_(k-1)[n] ).
Here R(theta) = [[cos, -sin],[sin, cos]], g_k = leak_g, and c_k = c_prev for k=2 (zero for k=1). Quantizer input q[n] = sum_k ff_k*u_k[n] + d_x*x[n]. Quantizer: q' = kq*q; y = clip(step*(floor(q'/step)+0.5), -1, 1) with step = 2/7 (eight levels, +/-1/7, 3/7, 5/7, 1). Nominal kq = 1. The quantizer uses the current q[n], so the loop has no extra delay beyond the one in the stage update. theta = 2*pi*f/fs, so 160 kHz is 0.3927 rad.

Model-form variation. Different implementations differ in how the resonance and loss land. Treat the effective theta_k as theta_k*(1+delta_k), delta_k in [-1.5%, +1.5%], independently per stage. Treat effective loss as g_k*(1-eps), eps in [0, 0.005]. Treat input gains b_x, b_f, c as scaled by (1+gamma), gamma in [-5%, +5%], common to the loop. These ranges, together with kq in [0.8, 1.25], define the R1 corner space. Tone frequencies and the offset values inside these ranges are sampled by the verifier at points you are not told, including interior points.

Noise (input-referred, added to x[n]). Per-sample white variance = 2*kB*T/C_in + (opamp rms)^2, in V^2, divided by fs_volts^2. Flicker has one-sided PSD Kf/f (V^2/Hz), generated for frequencies from about 1 kHz up to fs/2. Chopping multiplies the flicker PSD by 0.05 and the white variance by 1.2. The noise scale factor multiplies all noise amplitudes (variances scale as its square).

SNDR definition. Take a 32768-sample record after settling, coherent or Blackman-Harris windowed. Signal power is the tone's bins within +/-3 bins of the peak. Noise plus distortion is the sum of all other bins whose frequency is inside 150 to 170 kHz. SNDR is the ratio in dB. Average the spectrum of the output code stream (y values) over at least 8 records of independent noise draws.

State rms is sqrt(mean of u_k^2 + v_k^2 over all stages and samples in the window). R3 windows use a tone frequency that is an exact bin of the 4096-sample window. The fundamental's phase is the angle of the DFT bin at that frequency, referenced to the input tone phase.

Practice (ranges, not instructions). A 4th-order bandpass loop at an oversampling ratio of 64 with a multibit quantizer usually reaches 70 to 90 dB SQNR for ideal zeros. Pole radius close to 1 gives slow decay: the time constant is about 1/(1-r) cycles. Lightly damped resonators move the closed-loop poles strongly with small angle errors, and settling and phase consistency can change by large factors for 1% angle shifts. Quantization-noise spectral density depends on the zero spread across the band. kT at 300 K is about 4.14e-21 J.

Limits are in the brief. SNDR figures here are provisional estimates; the stated limits govern.
tasks.review:
### 28 · Narrowband resonator delta-sigma loop filter — advance, rank 7

Design decision as written: yes — "We need a loop-filter design for a narrowband sensor-readout converter ... the loop filter is built from at most two resonator stages" plus "deliver /app/output/design.json with these fields: n_res ... stages ... ff ... d_x; c_in_pf; chopping".

Forge task: Choose n_res (1 or 2), per-stage theta_rad, leak_g, b_x, b_f, c_prev, feedforward weights ff, d_x, c_in_pf and the chopping flag so that a 20 kHz band centred on a 160 kHz carrier at a 2.56 MHz clock holds in-band SNDR inside 68-74 dB and satisfies settling, phase/amplitude consistency, burst recovery and overload limits (R2-R5) under per-stage resonance-angle offsets up to +/-1.5%, input-gain spread +/-5%, quantizer gain 0.8-1.25x, up to 0.5% extra resonator loss and noise at 1.0x and 1.5x, with no trimming or digital calibration, and all coefficients inside R6 bounds.

Why it fits:
- It is a design decision, not an analysis: the deliverable is a parameter set (configuration design) for a loop filter, not a measurement or a solver.
- The handbook gives complete discrete-time state equations, quantizer law, noise model and SNDR definition, so a headless Python/numpy simulator can evaluate every requirement deterministically once corner points, seeds and noise draws are fixed.
- The artifact is a single JSON of ~10 bounded numbers; search and verification fit one agent run if the simulator is fast.
- The engineering difficulty is real: robust loop design where damping, zero spread and loop gain trade against SNDR floor/ceiling, settling, phase consistency and overload.

What stops it:
- Structural objections: none identified. The idea is a design decision, and the model is specified in enough detail to simulate.
- Unresolved feasibility risks (author claims, not verified): the reference outline is a proposed solution whose own text says "thresholds are provisional until a passing reference is run"; the feasible window may be empty or razor-thin with only two resonators when the 68 dB floor must hold at 1.5x noise and worst-case angle/loss/kq corners while the 74 dB ceiling must hold at favourable corners; R3's 0.5 deg phase std and 0.1 dB window-to-window amplitude limits at 1.5x noise may be noise-limited rather than design-limited; the three "public design" failure claims are hypotheses with no measured margins.
- Runtime is an estimate only: the corner/interior sample count and Monte Carlo cost are unspecified, and 8 noise draws x 32768 samples per condition across many conditions can dominate a two-hour budget.

How to check it:
- Python/numpy (bespoke simulator, not one of the tabulated tools): parse design.json, enforce R6 bounds and types; implement the handbook loop, quantizer and noise; sweep the declared corner grid plus random interior samples of delta_k, gamma, kq, eps, noise scale and held-out tone frequencies in 150-170 kHz.
- SNDR from 32768-sample output-code spectra averaged over 8 independent noise draws (R1); quantizer overload fraction and peak states (R5); state-rms ratio cycles 1500-2000 vs 8000-16000 from zero and random initial states (R2); phase std and amplitude change over 8 coherent 4096-cycle windows at 1.5x noise (R3); 200-cycle 1.2 FS burst recovery and post-3000-cycle SNDR (R4).
- The simulator itself needs independent validation (a second implementation of the same loop, or a textbook bandpass delta-sigma NTF/SNR check) before its verdicts count.

Simulation gaps:
- The model is normalized and behavioural: no finite opamp DC gain, GBW, slew, switch charge injection, clock jitter, quantizer metastability or capacitor-ratio mismatch; only the lumped given noise terms are represented.
- kT/C and flicker are applied as specified, but the mapping from c_in_pf to a real switched-capacitor or Gm-C resonator, and whether +/-1.5% resonance spread is realistic on-chip, is not checked.
- SNDR averaged over 8 noise draws carries Monte Carlo noise that may be comparable to the stated 0.2 dB grading resolution; the pass/fail rule at the 68/74 dB boundary needs defining.
- Interior-corner sampling density decides pass/fail and is unspecified; a design can pass a coarse grid and fail held-out points.
- Checkable in principle is not the same as implemented and validated: no simulator has been run or inspected here.

Why frontier models fail:
- Narrow robust-feasibility window: tuning leak toward 1 and zeros to the carrier raises nominal SNDR but makes settling, phase consistency and recovery collapse under ~1% angle shifts; heavy damping forfeits the 68 dB floor.
- Per-stage independent angle offsets combined with interior kq, loss and gain spread mean corner-only tuning fails; the agent must reason about the whole Monte Carlo envelope of a nonlinear clipped multibit loop, where no closed-form NTF argument covers overload recovery or state excursions.
- Coupled requirements (SNDR ceiling and floor, settling ratio, windowed phase/amplitude, overload fraction) must hold simultaneously; trade-offs are not separable per stage.

Real-world risks:
- A model-level pass need not survive a real implementation; coefficient spread, finite gain and thermal noise in an actual 2.56 MHz switched-capacitor loop could break R1/R2.
- The stated 68 dB floor at 1.5x noise in an 8-level, OSR-64 bandpass converter may be close to the achievable SQNR plus thermal-noise budget without trimming.
- Untrimmed +/-1.5% resonance-angle spread may be optimistic for on-chip RC/Gm tolerances; the reverse risk (spec too loose to be meaningful) also exists.

Milestones (if too big): not required at this stage; if the corner budget proves large, split as: 1. nominal-model coefficient design: grader checks R1 at nominal and R6 bounds; 2. robustness sweep: grader checks R1-R3 across the corner/interior set; 3. overload and recovery: grader checks R4-R5 plus full R1 rerun.

What to change (reshape):
- Nothing structural. Pin down (in Numbers to supply next) the enumeration of "every R1 condition", the held-out sampling and seed policy, the initial-state distribution, R2/R4 settling indexing, R3 window placement and phase wrapping, and the borderline SNDR rule.

Numbers to supply next:

- Requirement (missing spec): noise Monte Carlo policy — e.g. 8 records x 32768 samples per condition as stated, and a pass/fail rule when the mean SNDR lands within 0.2 dB of 68 or 74 dB.
- Requirement (missing spec): R2 initial-state distribution and measurement indexing — e.g. each u_k, v_k drawn uniformly in +/-0.3 FS, N seeds (e.g. 20), settling time zero at n=0, windows as written.

tasks.brief:
I need the 1.8 V core rail for our burst-mode radio/processor board. The load pulls periodic current bursts through a long, inductive feed. The rail has to come up the same way after a cold start, after a brownout where the capacitors still hold charge, and when the burst rate drifts. I need a passive decoupling and damping network from you.

Fixed inputs:
- Feed: ideal 1.90 V source, 0.02 ohm in series with 800 nH, switched on at t = 0. It feeds node A.
- Trace from node A to the load pins (node B): 100 nH in series with 10 mohm. You may add a series resistor Rs, 0 to 0.5 ohm, in this path.
- Load at node B: ideal current source, 0 to 1.2 A bursts, 35% duty, 20 ns rise and fall. Burst repetition frequency can be anywhere from 180 to 260 kHz. The load is already running at t = 0.
- Capacitors come from the classes in /app/input_assets/capacitor_classes.json (C, ESR, ESL, bias factor and area per part). Place them at node A or node B, at most 12 in total including any damper capacitors, and at most 60 mm2 total area. The optional damper is a series resistor Rd (0 to 1 ohm) plus capacitors of one class at node A.
- Passive parts only; no regulating element.
- Tolerances, applied in any combination: capacitance -20% to +10%, ESR +/-30%, series inductance (feed and trace together) +/-20%.
- Start states: all capacitors at 0 V (cold start), or all capacitors at one common residual voltage anywhere from 0 to 1.5 V, with zero inductor current (brownout recovery).

Requirements, at node B and valid for every start state, every burst frequency in the band and every tolerance combination. Bursts are numbered from 1 at t = 0.
1. Per-burst minimum voltage during bursts 60 to 80: at least 1.74 V.
2. Maximum voltage during bursts 60 to 80: at most 1.98 V.
3. Maximum voltage during the first 60 bursts: at most 2.10 V.
4. Difference between consecutive per-burst minima during bursts 60 to 80: at most 3 mV.
5. For identical frequency and tolerances, the spread of per-burst minima between cold start and any residual-charge start, during bursts 70 to 80: at most 4 mV.
6. Network limits: the count, area, Rs and Rd limits above, with classes from the supplied table only.

Deliverable: /app/output/design.json with these fields:
- "rs_ohm": number.
- "capacitors": list of {"class": string, "node": "A" or "B", "count": integer}.
- "damper": null, or {"class": string, "count": integer, "rd_ohm": number}.

The damper's capacitors count toward the 12-part and 60 mm2 limits.
tasks.handbook:
Conventions and data for the rail.

Capacitor model. Each capacitor is a series R-L-C branch from its node to ground. Its effective capacitance is C_eff = C_nominal x bias_factor x (1 + cap_offset), where the bias factor is the derating at the 1.8 V rail. ESR and ESL come from the table. The ESR offset scales ESR only. The series-inductance offset scales the feed 800 nH and the trace 100 nH by the same factor; the resistances are not scaled. For the damper, Rd is in series with each damper capacitor's own ESR. A count of n means n identical parts in parallel. Capacitors start at the stated common initial voltage and inductors at zero current.

Load waveform. For burst period T = 1/f, the current rises linearly from 0 to 1.2 A over 0 to 20 ns. It holds 1.2 A until 0.35 T, falls linearly to 0 over the next 20 ns, and stays at 0 until T. Burst k covers (k-1)T to kT. The per-burst minimum and maximum are the extreme node-B voltages in that interval.

Numerical consistency. Each per-burst minimum and maximum at node B must be resolved accurately enough that refining the time resolution by a factor of two changes it by at most 2 mV, in every case above.

Tolerance combinations. Offsets can lie anywhere in the stated ranges, not only at the endpoints. Burst frequency can take any value in 180 to 260 kHz.

Physics worth knowing. The feed inductance and the bulk capacitance form a series RLC with characteristic impedance Z0 = sqrt(L/C). Its damping ratio is zeta = (R/2) x sqrt(C/L). A step into this circuit gives overshoot that falls with zeta, and a stored residual decays with time constant about 2L/R. Ceramic classes lose much of their capacitance under DC bias. Polymer classes are mostly flat but have higher ESR and ESL. A resistor in series with a capacitor at node A damps the mode without carrying the load's DC current. A series resistor in the load path does carry that current and costs voltage during bursts.

DC reference. Average load current is 0.42 A. The burst-on current is 1.2 A. The total DC loop resistance without added parts is 30 mohm.

Feasibility note. The limits in the brief are provisional estimates and have not been confirmed with a passing reference design.
tasks.review:
### 05-burst-rail-decoupling-start-independent — burst rail decoupling and damping network — advance, rank 7

Design decision as written: yes — "I need a passive decoupling and damping network from you" with deliverable "\"rs_ohm\": number; \"capacitors\": list of {class, node 'A'|'B', count}; \"damper\": null or {class, count, rd_ohm}"

Forge task: Select the passive network for the 1.8 V burst-load core rail (Rs in the A→B trace, capacitor classes and counts from the supplied table at node A and node B, optional Rd+cap damper at node A, ≤12 parts, ≤60 mm²) so that node-B per-burst minima/maxima meet R1–R5 for every start state, every burst frequency in 180–260 kHz and every tolerance combination, with R7 timestep convergence; deliver the network as /app/output/design.json.

Why it fits:
• A configuration design decision (topology + discrete part selection + one series damping element) with a machine-readable output, not an analysis report.
• Fully checkable in principle with ngspice alone: the whole plant is ideal sources, series R-L, R-L-C capacitor branches and a piecewise-linear current load; a transient run yields per-burst extrema at node B directly.
• The difficulty is genuine engineering: a series RLC mode (zeta = (R/2)sqrt(C/L)) that must be damped enough for the 2.10 V start-up limit and the 3 mV/4 mV history rows, while damping elements must not eat the 1.74 V droop budget (30 mohm nominal loop plus 1.2 A burst edges).
• Robustness requirements (interior tolerance points, a whole frequency band, residual-charge starts from 0–1.5 V) force corner reasoning rather than a nominal-only tune; the 12-part / 60 mm² budget creates a real packaging/sizing trade-off between bulk at A and local ceramics at B.

What stops it:
• Structural: nothing structural blocks the task — it is a design decision, and the required physics is all linear RLC transient behaviour.
• Unresolved feasibility risks: (a) no passing reference design has been run — the brief itself says the limits are provisional; it is unknown whether any arrangement in the class table meets R1–R5 simultaneously (the R1 droop vs R3/R4/R5 damping window may be empty or razor-thin). (b) Grader runtime is unmeasured: 80 bursts at 180 kHz span ~0.45 ms; a timestep fine enough to resolve 20 ns edges and satisfy R7's 2 mV convergence, repeated over tolerance corners + interior points × frequencies × start states × two timesteps, could be tens to hundreds of runs. (c) The claim that naive designs fail (R3/R4/R5) is an author hypothesis, not inspected evidence.

How to check it:
• ngspice: parse design.json, build the netlist (1.90 V source, 0.02 Ω + 800 nH feed, 100 nH + 10 mΩ trace plus Rs, R-L-C branches per part from the class table with C_eff = C·bias_factor·(1+cap_offset), damper Rd in series with damper ESR, piecewise-linear 0→1.2 A burst current with 20 ns edges at 35% duty), run transient from cold start and from each residual voltage, and extract per-burst min/max at node B for bursts 1–80; enforce R1–R5 over the tolerance/frequency/start-state grid and R7 by repeating at half timestep.
• Static checks (script): class/node validity, part count ≤12 including damper, area sum ≤60 mm², 0 ≤ Rs ≤ 0.5 Ω, 0 ≤ Rd ≤ 1 Ω.

Simulation gaps:
• Linear RLC + ideal current source omits capacitor DC-bias nonlinearity beyond the table's fixed bias_factor, temperature dependence, ESL mutual coupling between branches, PCB plane spreading inductance/resistance, load-regulator interaction and any real source impedance of the 1.90 V feed.
• Per-burst extrema of a 20 ns-edge waveform are timestep-sensitive; R7 only bounds the change under one halving, not convergence to the true value. Trapezoidal ringing in ngspice can pollute sub-mV minima; the checker's own timestep must be stated and justified.
• Corner + random-interior tolerance sampling cannot prove the requirement holds for 'any combination' of offsets; passing the grid is evidence of robustness, not proof over the continuous box.

Why frontier models fail: plausibly (hypothesis, not tested) because the design couples a lightly damped feed mode to edge-local droop at node B, must hold across a continuous tolerance box, a 180–260 kHz band and a family of residual-charge initial states, and the fix for history persistence (more damping) directly worsens the burst droop limit — so a nominal-parameter or single-warm-start check passes while the low-C / high-L / low-ESR corner plus residual start breaks R4/R5. The task also demands the solver run and interpret its own sweeps and retune, not just emit a plausible recipe.

Real-world risks:
• The 60 mm² budget assumes the class table's area per part is a fair proxy for footprint plus keep-out; real placement at node B limits local ceramic count, and ESL of the shared via/ground path is not modelled.
• Bias derating is applied as a fixed factor at 1.8 V; during the 2.10 V startup transient and the 1.74 V droop the effective capacitance actually varies.
• 'All capacitors at one common residual voltage' is an idealisation of a brownout; real boards show non-uniform residuals and non-zero inductor current.

Milestones (if measured runtime forces a split):
1. Cold-start nominal network: design.json meeting R1–R3 at nominal tolerances and band corners — grader runs nominal cold-start transients only.
2. Tolerance-robust network: same deliverable meeting R1–R4 across the tolerance box — grader adds corner and interior tolerance points.
3. Start-independent network: full R1–R7 including residual-charge starts and timestep halving — grader adds G3 and G4.

What to change (reshape): nothing yet; keep the single task. Split into the milestones above only if measured ngspice runtimes show the full sweep exceeds the run budget.

Evidence status: author draft only. The capacitor class table is supplied as embedded text (it establishes specified data, not that /app/input_assets/capacitor_classes.json exists or is valid). The reference outline is a proposed approach, not a passing design. The 'public_designs' failure claims, the mechanism-survival narrative, and the provisional limits are unverified author claims; no simulation has been run or inspected. Distinguish: R1–R7 and the class table are stated requirements/data; feasibility, failure modes and the narrowness of the design window are engineering inferences awaiting execution evidence.

Checks before full-task readiness:
• Reproduce a baseline failure: run at least one naive recipe (e.g. maximum polymer bulk with no damping) and confirm the claimed R3/R4/R5 breakage at the low-C/high-L/low-ESR corner with a residual-charge start.
• Demonstrate one passing design.json under the checker's own grid before freezing limits; if none exists in the class table, report that honestly rather than widening R1–R5.
• Measure ngspice runtime and timestep convergence on the final grid (single run wall time, total sweep time, and the R7 2 mV margin in practice, including trapezoidal ringing behaviour).
• Fix the grader's timestep pair, extremum extraction window, tolerance/frequency/residual sampling sets and area accounting so R7 is deterministic.
• Confirm the design.json schema (number formatting, damper null semantics, whether damper caps sit at node A) is unambiguous for the parser.

Numbers to supply next:
• Requirement (verification still needed): a demonstrated passing design within the stated limits — e.g. a design.json that passes a full grid sweep, plus the baseline failure run above; limits themselves are already specified and must not be relaxed to obtain a pass.
• Requirement (specification): grader timestep pair and extremum extraction — e.g. dt = 2 ns and 1 ns, extrema taken over the exact burst-k interval [(k-1)T, kT], interpolation rule at interval endpoints stated.
• Requirement (specification): tolerance and frequency sampling — e.g. all 8 sign corners of (cap_offset, ESR_offset, L_offset) plus 20 fixed-seed interior points, frequencies {180, 197, 213, 233, 260} kHz plus 3 fixed-seed interior frequencies, residual voltages {0, 0.4, 0.9, 1.5} V plus 4 fixed-seed values in 0–1.5 V; state whether the damper capacitors share the same common residual (assumed yes).
• Requirement (specification): area and counting rules — e.g. total area = Σ (class area × count) including damper caps, hard limit 60 mm²; counts are positive integers; Rs/Rd defaults of 0 allowed; capacitors must be listed at most once per (class, node) row.
• Interface: inputs = /app/input_assets/capacitor_classes.json (as embedded in the brief) and the brief text; output = /app/output/design.json with exactly {"rs_ohm": number, "capacitors": [{"class": string, "node": "A"|"B", "count": integer}], "damper": null | {"class": string, "count": integer, "rd_ohm": number}} — e.g. {"rs_ohm": 0.05, "capacitors": [{"class": "P330", "node": "A", "count": 2}, {"class": "X47", "node": "B", "count": 4}], "damper": {"class": "X10", "count": 2, "rd_ohm": 0.35}}.
• Interface: checker netlist contract — e.g. ground node 0, node A and node B named as in the brief, ideal 1.90 V source switched on at t = 0 with zero initial inductor currents; a sample reference netlist line per branch.
• Handbook data: the capacitor class table is already supplied (e.g. X47: 47 uF, 3 mohm, 1.2 nH, 9 mm², bias 0.5); if real parts are intended later, add package/height limits and manufacturer bias-curve data. Verification still needed: confirm that per-branch C_eff, ESR, ESL and the shared L-scaling rule are implemented identically in agent and checker models.
• Verification still needed: budget check — measured wall time of one full G2+G3+G4 sweep vs the ~2 h agent budget (e.g. 60 runs × measured seconds each).

tasks.brief:
We are specifying a clocked sampling latch for our front end and need your sizing to meet our datasheet numbers. The topology is fixed (cross-coupled inverter latch, input pair, clocked tail, clocked reset pull-ups, output load capacitors; described in the handbook). You choose the values. Fixed inputs are in /app/input_assets/input.json (burst, beat, noise and thermal numbers) and /app/input_assets/mos_model.lib (device model).

Fixed conditions: supply 0.9 V nominal, also tested at 0.828 V (-8%); clock period 400 ps, 50% duty, 20 ps edges; burst of 4096 events. Events 1-3584 use the nominal overdrive in input.json with the stated beat modulation; events 3585-4096 use the 10x lower overdrive. Latch bias self-heats through the stated first-order thermal model driven by the latch's own dissipation.

Decision time t_d[k] is the time from the clock evaluation edge to the differential output reaching 90% of supply. Our residual metric is the RMS, over events 501-3584, of t_d[k] minus the least-squares fit of exactly two components: A*sin(2*pi*f_b*k*T + phi) with free A and phi at the beat frequency f_b in input.json, plus one constant. Nothing else is removed from the series. It is averaged over noise realizations.

Requirements, each at both supplies unless stated:
1. Residual RMS <= 1.2 ps (noise realizations other than those listed in input.json will be used).
2. Nominal-overdrive events: t_d <= 160 ps (40% of the period) for every event 1-3584.
3. Low-overdrive events 3585-4096: every event reaches 90% of supply before the end of its evaluate phase; zero unresolved events.
4. Before each evaluation, residual precharge error at the outputs <= 1 mV.
5. Average supply power over the burst <= 120 uW.
6. Peak tail current <= 300 uA.
7. Sum of all device widths (counting every device instance) <= 40 um; every channel length >= 30 nm.

Deliver /app/output/design.json with these fields: for each of the input pair, the cross-coupled NMOS pair, the cross-coupled PMOS pair, the tail device and the reset pull-ups, a width_um and a length_nm; tail_gate_bias_v; reset_release_offset_ps (reset release relative to the rising clock edge, -50 to +50); load_cap_ff (per output, 0 to 30).
tasks.handbook:
Topology (all values symmetric between the two sides): input pair Min1/Min2 (NMOS, gates driven by +/- half the differential input around 0.45 V common mode) with sources joined to the drain of tail NMOS Mt; Mt source to ground, gate = clock-high level switched between 0 and tail_gate_bias_v (0.35-0.9 V). Cross-coupled NMOS Mn1/Mn2 stacked on the input pair drains (outputs X, Y); cross-coupled PMOS Mp1/Mp2 from X, Y to supply; reset PMOS Mr1/Mr2 from X, Y to supply, gate = clock (on when clock low, precharging outputs to supply). Load cap load_cap_ff from each output to ground in addition to device parasitics. Evaluate phase = clock high (200 ps); reset phase = clock low. Decision threshold: |X-Y| >= 0.9*supply... equivalently the falling output below 10% of supply while the other stays high. Unresolved = threshold not reached before clock falls.

Device model: simple square-law with channel-length modulation, gate-oxide capacitance from tox and overlap capacitances; parameters in mos_model.lib. Self-heating: junction rise dT[k] obeys Cth*d(dT)/dt = P(t) - dT/Rth, with Rth = 2e5 K/W, Cth = 1e-11 F (time constant 2 us, comparable to the 1.64 us burst), so the dissipation sets a roughly linear-in-time bias drift over the burst. Threshold shifts -1.0 mV/K and mobility follows the simulator temperature law; temperature in the simulator = 27 C + dT.

Noise (values in input.json): input-referred thermal noise variance on the sampled node ~ gamma*k*T/C_node, gamma about 1-2, C_node the total output-node capacitance; flicker input-referred voltage PSD = KF/(Cox*W*L*f) for the input pair, exponent 1, integrated across 1/(4096*T) to 1/(2T). A noise voltage v_n shifts decision time by about -tau_reg*v_n/DeltaV_in where tau_reg = C_node/gm_regen is the regeneration time constant; t_d ~ tau_reg*ln(0.9*Vdd/(gain*DeltaV)). Sampling-latch practice: tau_reg of 8-25 ps for 0.9 V, 30 nm class logic. Larger tail current shortens tau_reg and raises dissipation and therefore self-heating; reset release timing sets the initial output imbalance and precharge completeness. Peak tail current in a dynamic latch typically sits at the start of evaluation.

Metric note: the residual after removing only the beat and a constant retains any slow monotonic drift of t_d across events 501-3584, and the harmonics of the beat modulation. Report conventions: ps, RMS = sqrt(mean(r^2)).
tasks.review:
### 22 · Sampling latch with bounded decision-time residual — advance, rank 7

Design decision as written: yes — "You choose the values… for each of the input pair, the cross-coupled NMOS pair, the cross-coupled PMOS pair, the tail device and the reset pull-ups, a width_um and a length_nm; tail_gate_bias_v; reset_release_offset_ps …; load_cap_ff". The deliverable is a parameter vector that fixes a physical cell implementation, not an analysis.

Forge task: Size a fixed-topology clocked sampling latch (5 device groups × W/L, tail gate bias, reset release offset, per-output load cap) in a 0.9 V, 400 ps process so that, across both supplies and a 4096-event burst with self-heating drift and noise, the decision-time residual after removing only a beat sinusoid and a constant is ≤ 1.2 ps, all nominal events decide within 160 ps, all 10x-lower-overdrive events resolve, precharge error ≤ 1 mV, average power ≤ 120 µW, peak tail current ≤ 300 µA, and total width ≤ 40 µm with L ≥ 30 nm.

Why it fits:
• It is a real parameter-selection design problem: the delivered design.json fully determines a buildable cell, and every requirement is a property of that geometry/bias.
• The physics is genuinely coupled: tail current shortens tau_reg (helping R2/R3) but raises dissipation, which drives the first-order thermal drift that the two-component residual explicitly does not remove (hurting R1), while width/length set flicker noise area and power. Reset release offset trades initial imbalance against precharge completeness (R4). This is the kind of trade-space frontier models handle poorly without a disciplined simulation loop.
• The metric trap is real and stated honestly: a solver that fits a linear or polynomial term absorbs the drift and optimizes toward high-tail designs that fail the specified two-term fit. R1 also bounds power-side cheating.
• The task is self-contained: topology, model card, burst definition, bounds and output schema are all specified text.

What stops it (structural objections vs. feasibility risks):
• Structural: none fatal at Stage 1 — the idea is a design decision with a plausible headless check path.
• Unresolved feasibility risk — numerical noise floor: the residual limit is 1.2 ps while t_d is extracted from a transient crossing on a 400 ps clock. ngspice timestep/tolerance settings are not specified; interpolation error and solver noise could be of the same order as the limit, making the metric unmeasurable or seed-dependent. Needs a measured noise floor (rerun one candidate twice with tightened reltol/tstep and compare t_d series).
• Unresolved feasibility risk — noise model underdetermination: the handbook gives input-referred formulas with "about" language ("gamma about 1-2", a shift of "about -tau_reg*v_n/DeltaV_in"), and it is unspecified whether noise perturbs t_d post hoc or is injected as circuit noise. The grader's held-out-seed behavior cannot be predicted precisely until this mapping is nailed down.
• Unresolved feasibility risk — runtime: the grader plan implies transient sweeps over a (supply, dT, overdrive) grid plus event-by-event thermal stepping and ≥10 noise seeds, done inside the agent's own loop for candidate designs. 30-50 candidate evaluations at an unknown per-evaluation cost could exceed the ~2 h budget. Estimate arithmetic: a 4096-event per-event transient is clearly infeasible; the grid-plus-interpolation approach is required, and its fidelity is unproven.
• Unresolved feasibility risk — reference feasibility: the reference_outline explicitly states no passing reference has been demonstrated, and the residual limit is marked provisional. Whether any sizing exists inside the 7-requirement window is an open question, not an established fact.

How to check it:
• ngspice (headless, .tran) with the supplied level-1 models: builds the latch netlist from design.json; extracts per-event t_d (output threshold crossing), precharge error at end of reset, tail current waveform, and per-event energy.
• Python (numpy least squares): fits exactly [sin(2*pi*f_b*k*T), cos(2*pi*f_b*k*T), 1] over events 501-3584 and computes residual RMS, averaged over held-out seeds; steps the first-order thermal model (Rth=2e5 K/W, Cth=1e-11 F) event by event from measured energy and applies the -1.0 mV/K threshold shift and the stated mobility law.
• Schema/bounds check (pure parsing) for R7.

Simulation gaps:
• Level-1 square-law at 30 nm channel lengths omits velocity saturation, DIBL, subthreshold conduction, and real short-channel gm behavior; a design passing here may not behave the same in a real 30 nm process.
• The single-pole self-heating model with uniform junction temperature ignores spatial thermal gradients and package effects.
• Post-hoc noise perturbation (if that is the intended method) does not capture noise-modified regeneration dynamics or the correlation between noise and the thermal state; in-sim noise is stochastic and needs many repetitions.
• Grid-interpolated t_d vs. per-event simulation can hide beat-phase-dependent effects; corner coverage (supply × dT × overdrive × seeds) is asserted, not demonstrated.

Why frontier models fail (hypothesis, not trial-verified):
• The natural shortcut — fit away the slow drift or optimize tau_reg alone — fails the exactly-two-component residual held out from the agent's own fit.
• Meeting R2/R3 (regeneration speed at 2 mV overdrive, worst supply) pushes toward larger tail current, which violates R1/R5/R6 via self-heating; the viable window is narrow and requires disciplined multivariable search, not one-shot sizing.
• Beat-harmonic content and event-window selection (501-3584) reward actual per-event simulation over analytic estimation.

Real-world risks:
• Square-law model fidelity (above) is the dominant gap; also the noise formulas are textbook approximations, and Rth/Cth are stylized.
• A design that passes this grader is validated against the stated models only, not against silicon or a PDK.

Evidence status: Everything in the payload is a draft/specification and author claim. Specifically unverified: the public_designs failure narratives (R1 drift "several times 1.2 ps", R2/R3 and R5/R6 failures), the stated margins, the reference_outline strategy, and all runtime/budget implications. Verified evidence supplied: only the text of input.json, mos_model.lib, the requirement list and the grader plan. No simulation output, netlist, or passing design artifact exists in the input.

Checks before full-task readiness:
1. Define precisely: t_d threshold (falling output < 10% Vdd vs |X-Y| ≥ 0.9 Vdd), beat modulation form, and the noise-to-t_d mapping (post-hoc vs in-sim).
2. Measure the numerical noise floor on t_d and on residual RMS with fixed ngspice options; confirm it is well under 1.2 ps (e.g., < 0.2 ps).
3. Reproduce one claimed public-design failure (e.g., a large-tail design exceeding the residual) to validate the grader pipeline end to end.
4. Demonstrate at least one design meeting all seven requirements under the grader's own settings, or confirm the window is empty at the provisional limits.
5. Time one full evaluation (grid + thermal stepping + seeds) to establish the candidate budget fits the run.

Milestones (if the full loop proves too big):
1. Static/per-event characterization task: given a fixed sizing, compute t_d grid vs. (Vdd, dT, overdrive) and energy per event; grader checks extraction accuracy against a slow high-accuracy reference run.
2. Residual-and-thermal task: given the grid, step the thermal model and produce the t_d series and residual; grader checks fit convention and RMS.
3. Full sizing task: deliver design.json meeting all seven requirements.

Numbers to supply next:
• Specification (missing): decision-time threshold definition — e.g., falling output crossing 0.1*Vdd, with interpolation rule; and whether R2/R3 use the same crossing for all seeds.
• Specification (missing): beat modulation expression — e.g., overdrive[k] = 20 mV * (1 + 0.1*sin(2*pi*7.3e6*k*400e-12)) applied to the differential input.
• Specification (missing): noise injection method and exact mapping to t_d — e.g., per-event delta t_d = -tau_reg*v_n/DeltaV_in with C_node = sum of node capacitances from the netlist; define v_n draw per seed and its units (KF = 2e-25 in what units).
• Requirement (provisional): confirm residual limit 1.2 ps and the 3% numerical margin; do not widen it to obtain a pass — instead report if the window is empty.
• Interface: input files /app/input_assets/input.json and mos_model.lib (as supplied); output /app/output/design.json with exactly the listed keys and units (width_um, length_nm, V, ps, fF); state whether extra keys are permitted and the float tolerance (draft says 1e-9).
• Handbook data: ngspice analysis settings — e.g., reltol 1e-6, max timestep 0.5 ps, tstart for settle; device counting convention (2 per pair/reset/input device, 1 tail) as in G1.
• Verification still needed: baseline failure reproduction for one public design; measured per-evaluation runtime; demonstrated passing design or an empty-window determination; noise-floor measurement.
• Handbook data (stated as practice, keep as guidance not requirement): tau_reg 8-25 ps for 0.9 V / 30 nm class; peak tail current occurs at start of evaluation.
